We complement this result with an $\Omega(\frac{n^2 \log n}{\varepsilon^2})$ lower bound for any non-adaptive algorithm, showing that our algorithm is almost tight in $n$ (within a $\log n$ factor).

authors.name: Flavio Chierichetti, Mirko Giacchini, Ravi Kumar, Silvio Lattanzi, Alessandro Panconesi, Erasmo Tani, Andrew Tomkins

papers.title: SpikingGamma: Temporally Precise Online SNN Training Through Smoothed Temporal Delays
papers.summary: Neuromorphic hardware implementations of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) promise energy-efficient, low-latency AI through sparse, event-driven computation. Yet, training SNNs under fine temporal discretization remains challenging, hindering low-latency responsiveness and the mapping of software-trained SNNs to efficient hardware. In current approaches, spiking neurons are modeled as self-recurrent units, embedded into recurrent networks to maintain state over time, and trained with BPTT or RTRL variants based on surrogate gradients. These methods scale poorly with temporal resolution, while online approximations exhibit instability for long sequences and tend to fail at capturing temporal patterns. To address these limitations, we develop SpikingGamma, an SNN architecture in which neurons maintain a compact bank of smoothed-delay states and communicate through sigma-delta spike-coding. We show that in feedforward networks, SpikingGamma supports direct online error backpropagation through the continuous reconstruction signal, avoiding surrogate gradients through the spike discontinuity. This enables stable learning of temporal patterns with minimal spiking and scales feedforward SNNs to complex tasks and benchmarks with competitive accuracy, all while remaining robust to the temporal resolution of the model. Our approach offers both an alternative to recurrent SNNs trained with surrogate gradients, and a novel route for mapping SNNs to neuromorphic hardware.

authors.name: Roel Koopman, Sebastian Otte, Sander Boht\'e

papers.title: Anytime-Valid Conformal Risk Control
papers.summary: Prediction sets provide a means of quantifying the uncertainty in predictive tasks. Using held out calibration data, conformal prediction and risk control can produce prediction sets that exhibit statistically valid error control in a computationally efficient manner. However, in the standard formulations, the error is only controlled on average over many possible calibration datasets of fixed size. In this paper, we extend the control to remain valid with high probability over a cumulatively growing calibration dataset at any time point. We derive such guarantees using quantile-based arguments and illustrate the applicability of the proposed framework to settings involving distribution shift. We further show that our guarantees are asymptotically tight, in the sense that the risks converge to the target level from below, and that the rate of our correction cannot be improved. Finally, we demonstrate the practical performance of our methods through both simulations and real-world numerical examples.

authors.name: Bror Hultberg, Dave Zachariah, Ant\^onio H. Ribeiro

papers.title: Wedge Sampling: Efficient Tensor Completion with Nearly-Linear Sample Complexity
papers.summary: We introduce wedge sampling, a non-adaptive sampling scheme for recovering an order-$k$ low-rank tensor of side length $n$ from structured observations of its entries. The scheme samples pairs of entries in the same column of a tensor unfolding, forming length-two paths (wedges) in the associated bipartite sampling graph. The products of the paired entries supply the row correlations needed for spectral initialization in regimes where uniform sampling yields too few wedges. For fixed rank, incoherence, tensor order, and condition number, wedge sampling enables polynomial-time recovery with nearly linear sample complexity in $n$. The spectral initializer can be combined with existing refinement procedures using only an additional $\tilde O(n)$ uniformly sampled entries. Spectral refinement achieves weak recovery to any fixed relative Frobenius error. For symmetric third-order tensors with incoherent canonical polyadic factors, gradient descent achieves exact recovery in the noiseless setting, with error decreasing geometrically. The improvement over the $\tilde O(n^{k/2})$ sample complexity typical of efficient methods under uniform entry sampling shows how the conjectured computational barrier depends on the observation model. A key ingredient for the gradient descent analysis is a concentration bound for sparse random tensors in an incoherent spectral norm. We also give error bounds for both procedures under additive Gaussian noise and explicit signal-to-noise conditions. Beyond tensor completion, the same sampling scheme improves the sample complexity of one-sided matrix completion, where the goal is to recover the left singular subspace of a matrix with many more columns than rows.

authors.name: Hengrui Luo, Anna Ma, Ludovic Stephan, Yizhe Zhu

papers.title: Privacy-Utility Tradeoffs with Quantum Local Differential Privacy
papers.summary: When sensitive information is encoded in data, it is important to ensure the privacy of information when attempting to learn useful information from the data. There is a natural tradeoff whereby increasing privacy requirements may decrease the utility of a learning protocol. In the quantum setting of differential privacy, such tradeoffs between privacy and utility have so far remained largely unexplored. In this work, we study optimal privacy-utility tradeoffs for both generic and application-specific utility metrics when privacy is quantified by $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-quantum local differential privacy. In the generic setting, we focus on optimizing fidelity and trace distance between the original state and the privatized state. We show that the depolarizing mechanism achieves the optimal utility for given privacy requirements. We then study the specific application of learning the expectation of an observable with respect to an input state when only given access to privatized states. We derive a lower bound on the number of samples of privatized data required to achieve a fixed accuracy guarantee with high probability. To prove this result, we employ existing lower bounds on private quantum hypothesis testing, thus showcasing the first operational use of them. We also devise private mechanisms that achieve optimal sample complexity with respect to the privacy parameters and accuracy parameters, demonstrating that utility can be significantly improved for specific tasks in contrast to the generic setting. In addition, we show that the number of samples required to privately learn observable expectation values scales as $\Theta((\varepsilon \beta)^{-2})$, where $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$ is the privacy parameter and $\beta$ is the accuracy tolerance. We conclude by initiating the study of private classical shadows, which promise useful applications for private learning tasks.

authors.name: Theshani Nuradha, Sujeet Bhalerao, Felix Leditzky

papers.title: SimVLA: Attributing Gains in VLA Models Through Controlled Ablation
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often bundle architectural changes with different pretraining data, backbone scales, and optimization recipes, obscuring what actually drives progress. We introduce SimVLA, a deliberately minimal VLA, a standard vision-language backbone with a lightweight continuous-action head, as a controlled testbed for this attribution problem; our contribution is methodological and empirical (a controlled attribution study and a minimal-baseline calibration), not a new technique. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, WidowX, and Google Robot, one-knob-at-a-time ablations show that training dynamics are the largest measured driver, producing performance swings of $\Delta$$\approx$54--94\%, while task configuration and architecture have smaller effects under matched settings. Despite using a small backbone and no additional large-scale robot-data VLA pretraining before benchmark-specific training, SimVLA reaches 98.6\% average success on LIBERO, remains competitive across the other benchmarks, and transfers to held-out real-robot scenes. These results suggest that simple, carefully controlled VLA baselines remain underexplored and provide a calibration point for future architectural claims within the VLM-encoder plus lightweight-head family. Website: https://frontierrobo.github.io/SimVLA

authors.name: Yuankai Luo, Woping Chen, Tong Liang, Zhenguo Li

papers.title: Convergence Rate of a Functional Learning Method for Conditional Stochastic Optimization
papers.summary: We consider a stochastic optimization problem involving two random variables: a context variable $X$ and a dependent variable $Y$. The objective is to minimize the expected value of a nonlinear loss functional applied to the conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[f(X, Y,\beta) \mid X]$, where $f$ is a nonlinear function and $\beta$ represents the decision variables. We focus on the practically important setting in which direct sampling from the conditional distribution of $Y \mid X$ is infeasible, and only a stream of i.i.d. observation pairs $\{(X^k, Y^k)\}_{k=0,1,2,\ldots}$ is available. In our approach, the conditional expectation is approximated within a prespecified parametric function class. We analyze a simultaneous learning-and-optimization algorithm that jointly estimates the conditional expectation and optimizes the outer objective. Using a specially designed measure of non-optimality, combining the squared norm of the objective function's gradient and the mean square error of the auxiliary parametric model, we establish that the method achieves a convergence rate of order $\mathcal{O}\big(1/\sqrt{N}\big)$, where $N$ denotes the number of observed pairs. The rate holds in expectation when the auxiliary model is linear in its parameters, which includes linear architectures with bounded features, and in probability for general smooth models.

authors.name: Noel Smith, Andrzej Ruszczynski

papers.title: Continuous-time learning of probability distributions: a case study in a digital trial of young children with type 1 diabetes
papers.summary: Understanding how biomarker distributions evolve over time is a central challenge in digital health and chronic disease monitoring. For example, in diabetes, changes in the distribution of glucose measurements can reveal patterns of disease progression and treatment response that conventional summary measures miss. Motivated by a 13-week clinical trial comparing the closed-loop insulin delivery system t:slim X2 with standard therapy in children with type 1 diabetes, we propose a probabilistic framework to model the continuous-time evolution of time-indexed distributions using continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data collected every five minutes. We represent the glucose distribution as a Gaussian mixture, with time-varying mixture weights governed by a neural ODE. We estimate the model parameters using a distribution-matching criterion based on the maximum mean discrepancy. The resulting framework is interpretable, computationally efficient, and sensitive to subtle temporal distributional changes. In the CGM trial data analyzed here, the method detects treatment-related improvements in glucose dynamics that are difficult to capture with traditional analytical approaches.

authors.name: Antonio \'Alvarez-L\'opez, Marcos Matabuena

papers.title: The Value of Information in Resource-Constrained Pricing
papers.summary: Dynamic pricing with resource constraints requires balancing exploration of unknown demand patterns against exploitation of known information to maximize revenue. We develop algorithms for this problem across different information regimes. Products share perishable resources, and the firm posts prices and observes the realized requests, which may exceed the remaining capacity. In the full-information setting, a residual-correction policy that solves the fluid problem once attains $O(\log T)$ regret with bounded prices and arbitrary-rank resource matrices. In the no-information setting, deterministic exploration followed by a certainty-equivalent policy attains $O(\sqrt T)$ regret when the limiting fluid solution is nondegenerate. In the informed-price setting, given an initial price-demand estimate, a feedback controller learns the implementing prices without estimating the slope matrix if the slope matrix is symmetric, a set containing it is known in advance, the informed price is aligned with the resource constraints, and an inverse-image condition holds. A selector chooses between the informed-price algorithm and the no-information algorithm from historical data. Its regret bound includes observation error, misalignment, inventory exits, and periods on the fixed price. We further show how offline surrogate models reduce the regret of the learning policy through variance reduction, even when misspecified. The bound includes calibration and screen failures, and the regret is reduced for all sufficiently large horizons. We finally demonstrate the empirical performances of our policies through complete numerical experiments.

authors.name: Ruicheng Ao, Jiashuo Jiang, David Simchi-Levi

papers.title: Component-Adaptive and Lesion-Level Supervision for Improved Small Structure Segmentation in Brain MRI
papers.summary: Small lesions in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are easily missed: a segmentation model can reach a high Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) while leaving many of them undetected. We ask whether this omission comes from the network or from the training objective. In multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation, nnU-Net trained with its default Dice and cross-entropy loss produces almost no response to most of the small lesions it misses, so no decision threshold recovers them, and four other architectures trained with the same loss detect no more of them. We therefore change only the objective. CATMIL adds two lesion-level terms to the nnU-Net loss: a Component-Adaptive Tversky (CAT) term, which gives each lesion a weight nearly independent of its size, and a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) term, which treats each lesion as a bag of voxels and penalizes any lesion in which no voxel is detected. On MSLesSeg, CATMIL raises small-lesion recall from 0.796 to 0.873 (difference 95\% CI +0.030 to +0.157) and misses 48\% fewer lesions, at comparable DSC. The gain holds on the cross-validation predictions of 47 further patients, for lesions of at least 3~mm, and on a second dataset trained with the same loss weights. CATMIL also detects more small lesions than CC-DiceCE, an instance-level loss that balances lesions within an overlap term (0.873 vs.\ 0.831), indicating that lesions must be supervised not only in proportion but also for their detection. The cost is additional small false-positive components; a component-size filter removes most of them, and at the lesion-wise precision of the default loss CATMIL still detects more small lesions. Code: https://github.com/luumsk/SmallLesionMRI.

authors.name: Minh Sao Khue Luu, Evgeniy N. Pavlovskiy, Bair N. Tuchinov

papers.title: Optimal algorithmic complexity of inference in quantum kernel methods
papers.summary: Quantum kernel methods are among the leading candidates for achieving quantum advantage in supervised learning. A key bottleneck is the cost of inference: evaluating a trained model on new data requires estimating a weighted sum $\sum_{i=1}^N \alpha_i k(x,x_i)$ of $N$ kernel values to additive precision $\varepsilon$, where $\alpha$ is the vector of trained coefficients. The standard approach estimates each term independently via sampling, yielding a query complexity of $O(N\lVert\alpha\rVert_2^2/\varepsilon^2)$. In this work, we identify two independent axes for improvement: (1) How individual kernel values are estimated (sampling versus quantum amplitude estimation), and (2) how the sum is approximated (term-by-term versus via a single observable), and systematically analyze all combinations thereof. The query-optimal combination, encoding the full inference sum as the expectation value of a single observable and applying quantum amplitude estimation, achieves a query complexity of $O(\lVert\alpha\rVert_1/\varepsilon)$, removing the dependence on $N$ from the query count and yielding a quadratic improvement in both $\lVert\alpha\rVert_1$ and $\varepsilon$. We prove a matching lower bound of $\Omega(\lVert\alpha\rVert_1/\varepsilon)$, establishing query-optimality of our approach up to logarithmic factors. Beyond query complexity, we also analyze how these improvements translate into gate costs and show that the query-optimal strategy is not always optimal in practice from the perspective of gate complexity. Our results provide both a query-optimal algorithm and a practically optimal choice of strategy depending on hardware capabilities, along with a complete landscape of intermediate methods to guide practitioners. All algorithms require only amplitude estimation as a subroutine and are thus natural candidates for early-fault-tolerant implementations.

authors.name: Elies Gil-Fuster, Seongwook Shin, Sofiene Jerbi, Jens Eisert, Maximilian J. Kramer

papers.title: Learning Curves and Prediction Persistence to Under-Regularization of Spectral Algorithms in Large Dimensions
papers.summary: We study how prediction risk changes as regularization is reduced for spectral algorithms when the sample size $n$ and dimension $d$ satisfy $n\asymp d^\gamma$ for fixed $\gamma>0$. For inner-product kernels on the sphere, under a source condition with smoothness $s\geq0$ and a signal nondegeneracy condition, we characterize the conditional excess risk up to constant factors at each fixed admissible scale $\lambda\asymp d^{-u}$, $u>0$, and at interpolation. The resulting risk orders describe the effects of source smoothness, filter qualification, and transitions between spectral blocks. They identify when the conditional excess risk retains the minimax risk order as regularization is weakened from an optimal scale to interpolation, and when an interval before interpolation exhibits a polynomially larger risk. We also compare the kernel risk with a population sequence risk for the same spectral filter, using a deterministic regularization scale bounded below by order $n^{-1}$. Finally, for noninteger $\gamma$, we extend the risk characterization for kernel ridge regression to kernels on general domains under spectral scaling, hyper-contractivity, and tail diagonal concentration conditions, together with the source and signal conditions.

authors.name: Weihao Lu, Qian Lin, Yingcun Xia, Dongming Huang

papers.title: Gradient Regularized Newton Boosting Trees with Global Convergence
papers.summary: Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs) dominate tabular machine learning, with modern implementations like XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost being based on Newton boosting: a second-order descent step in the space of decision trees. Despite its empirical success, the global convergence of Newton boosting is poorly understood compared to first-order boosting. In this paper, we introduce Restricted Newton Descent, a framework for convex optimization with Newton's method on Hilbert spaces with inexact iterates, based on the concepts of cosine angle and weak gradient edge. Within this framework, we recover Newton boosting with GBDTs and classical finite-dimensional theory as special cases. We first prove that vanilla Newton boosting achieves a linear rate of convergence for smooth, strongly convex losses that satisfy a Hessian-dominance condition. To handle general convex losses with Lipschitz Hessians, we extend a recent gradient regularized Newton scheme to the restricted weak learner setting, establishing the first global $\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{k^2})$ convergence rate for second-order GBDTs. This scheme minimally modifies the classical algorithm by introducing an adaptive $\ell_2$-regularization term proportional to the square root of the gradient norm at each iteration. In numerical experiments, we show that this scheme converges while vanilla Newton boosting may diverge.

authors.name: Nikita Zozoulenko, Daniel Falkowski, Thomas Cass, Lukas Gonon

papers.title: Survey-aware Machine Learning: A Guideline for Valid Population Health Inference based on Scoping Review
papers.summary: Machine Learning (ML) models trained on complex health surveys such as the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) often ignore primary sampling units, stratification variables, and sampling weights. This practice violates the independence assumptions of standard evaluation methods. As a result, estimates become biased, uncertainty is underestimated, and fairness assessments fail to reflect population-level disparities. We propose Survey-aware Machine Learning (SaML), a nine-step guideline that incorporates survey design metadata across the ML lifecycle. Through a scoping review of 16 methodological papers, we summarize existing work on weighted model training, design-based cross-validation, and survey-adjusted performance evaluation. We also identify gaps in hyperparameter tuning and deployment. We provide task-specific guidance that clarifies which steps are required for different analytical objectives. SaML provides a checklist for valid population inference from survey data.

authors.name: YongKyung Oh, Henry W. Zheng, Jeffrey Feng, Alex A. T. Bui

papers.title: Adaptive Inference for Resource-Constrained Dynamic Pricing
papers.summary: We study dynamic pricing over a finite selling horizon when limited resource capacity determines revenue and the observations available for inference at a prespecified price. Resource depletion can remove the target neighborhood from the feasible price set, changing the experiment generated by the pricing policy. We develop inference-aware re-solving controllers that check target-band feasibility before current covariates arrive and log the pricing mixture. Target-reserved and smooth controllers take population mean-pair geometry as a predeployment input; learned barycentric re-solving instead estimates stationary mean-consumption vectors of predeclared component kernels. On an affine binding-capacity family, an exact-input target-reserved controller assigning mass $t^{-\gamma}$ obtains an information clock of order $T^{1-\gamma}$ in probability, radius $O_p\{T^{-(1-\gamma)/2}\}$, and, under an exposed-face reward identity, a signed fluid-benchmark gap bounded above by $O(\log T+T^{1-\gamma})$. Under the exogenous affine-face condition, predeclared target support, and polynomial error spending with exponent greater than one, learned barycentric re-solving has a linear information clock in probability and an $O(\log T)$ signed-gap upper bound; centered local pricing has the same orders under slack capacity and global target optimality. An exact-input, target-compatible smooth alternative without reservation gives a linear clock in probability, an $O_p(T^{-1/2})$ deterministic-envelope radius with unconditional coverage and reporting probability tending to one, and an $O(\log^2 T)$ signed-gap upper bound. Boundary results show when physical support is lost and why a $1/t$ target branch yields only $O_p(1)$ information if it is the sole target-local source. The policy reports an interval when its prespecified support and information conditions hold and otherwise abstains.

authors.name: Ruicheng Ao, Jiashuo Jiang, David Simchi-Levi

papers.title: Automating the Expert Eye: A System-Agnostic Deep Learning Framework for Rare Event Discovery in Imbalanced Force Spectroscopy
papers.summary: Single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) probes biomolecular mechanics at the single-molecule level, but high-throughput acquisition of force-extension curves creates a data processing bottleneck. Identifying rare specific unbinding events among thousands of noise-dominated traces still relies largely on manual visual inspection. Here, we present a deep learning workflow for the preliminary screening of severely imbalanced SMFS datasets. Using 2D image representations of force-extension curves without system-specific physical priors, we fine-tuned a modified ResNet18 architecture trained with focal loss and evaluated it on the mechanical unfolding pathways of the Ruminococcus champanellensis XMod-Doc/Coh complex. On a held-out test set with a 1.34% target prevalence (13 positive P_2 events among 970 curves), the model achieved 92.31% recall (12 of 13 events) and 91.95% specificity (880 of 957 negative traces), automatically discarding 90.82% of the dataset and reducing manual review from 970 to 89 flagged curves. We also integrated Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) to provide a qualitative visual reference of the curve regions driving each prediction. The complete Python pipeline is released as open-source software with an executable Google Colab notebook, enabling reproducible SMFS screening without dedicated local GPU hardware.

authors.name: Jorge Rodriguez-Ramos

papers.title: What Does a Temporal Benchmark Score Measure? Decomposing Channel Use in Video VLM Evaluation
papers.summary: A score on a temporal video question answering benchmark is meant to measure that a model has temporal understanding, but it conflates two questions. (1) is the question even temporal, does it need several frames and their order? And (2) when it does, does the model recover the order from the pixels, or read it off the positional encoding (RoPE)? Most of a temporal score answers neither, since a single frame and answer priors often carry it, and the field's validity checks, frame-shuffle sensitivity and multi-frame gain, speak only to (1). For (2) we score a reversal conflict, frames reversed while RoPE stays forward, two ways: label-free, as the accuracy lost against the forward labels, and against reversed labels wherever labels transform deterministically under time reversal. This separates a model that follows the reversed content from one merely disrupted. The two readings dissociate two similarly scoring models at both model scales. Qwen3-VL answers the reversed event it actually sees, reading the visual sequence. Molmo2 correctly reports a backwards video when positions agree, and flipping only the RoPE indices flips its prediction to the forward events, i.e. it reads positions. We call these regimes visual-sequence-dominant and position-dominant. Controls show reversed content is processable whenever the channels agree, and that both families share a bias toward describing events as running forward (arrow-of-time prior) that, being similar in strength, cannot by itself account for the dissociation. The distinction matters because the two channels fail on opposite inputs: two models with the same score are not interchangeable.

authors.name: Farrukh Rahman

papers.title: D\'ej\`a Cue: Localizing States in Object Histories via Vocabulary-Relative Coordinates
papers.summary: Object tracking preserves identity through visual changes, but cannot tell when an object is whole, cut, or peeled. We study state-moment retrieval: locating when a tracked object exhibits each state in a supplied set of descriptions. However, absolute image--text similarity can favor shared object semantics, obscuring the distinctions needed to localize individual states. Our insight is that the alternatives themselves provide a reference for measuring state evidence. We introduce D\'ej\`a Cue, a training-free framework that centers description embeddings on a state-balanced vocabulary mean, producing query directions that compare each state against its alternatives. Using frozen vision--language encoders, D\'ej\`a Cue calibrates frame scores and retrieves intervals at multiple durations within contiguous visible runs. We construct MS-VOST by annotating 620 object histories with 2,465 states. With the encoder and temporal search fixed, D\'ej\`a Cue improves all three localization metrics over absolute scoring across eight encoder configurations, raising Top-1 temporal IoU by 0.42--1.14 percentage points. These gains persist across four text constructions, and candidate-ranking analysis shows that the vocabulary reference brings relevant intervals forward within the same search space. These results establish the supplied state vocabulary as an object-specific reference for localizing semantic states from frozen visual representations.

authors.name: Haofan Cao, Zhichao You, Yunkai Yang, Liang Guo, Jie Wang, Chongshou Li

papers.title: Achieving Near-Zero-Overhead Multi-Model Hierarchical Classification in Real-Time Detection Pipelines
papers.summary: Edge-deployed vision systems in target recognition, surveillance, autonomous vehicles, and drone domains require hierarchical inference pipelines where a detection model identifies objects of interest and downstream classifiers provide fine-grained attribute analysis. Running all models on the GPU creates a serial bottleneck that limits real-time throughput as pipeline stages grow. Modern edge SoCs pair GPUs with dedicated neural accelerators (NPUs, DLAs) capable of concurrent execution, yet deploying custom models on these accelerators remains impractical due to strict operator constraints, quantization incompatibilities, and an undocumented end-to-end pipeline. We target NVIDIA Jetson DLA cores as the representative platform. We present a five-step methodology for zero GPU fallback DLA INT8 deployment of classification backbones, comprising architecture adaptation, manual dynamic range workaround to rescue TensorRT's implicit quantization (recovering 94.0% accuracy from implicit quantization's 75%) for rapid pipeline validation before explicit quantization, quantization-aware training, ONNX graph surgery for DLA compilation, and a concurrent GPU-detection/DLA-classification inference pipeline. We document nine engineering constraints with root-cause analysis and generalizable solutions. Validation on a dual-head person attribute classifier running on DLA alongside a GPU object detector on a Jetson Orin NX demonstrates near-zero pipeline overhead (12.5 vs. 13.3~FPS detector-only at 1080p), with dual-DLA scaling at no additional cost. The methodology is backbone-agnostic and generalizes to any detection-classification edge pipeline.

authors.name: Vaishnav Raju

papers.title: Silver Rate Is (Almost) Optimal for Gradient Descent
papers.summary: Gradient descent (GD) is one of the most fundamental algorithms in optimization. Yet even for smooth convex objectives, the optimal rate among predetermined nonnegative stepsize schedules has remained unresolved. Altschuler and Parrilo [Mathematical Programming, 2025] showed that their recursive silver stepsize schedule achieves an $O(n^{-p_{\mathrm{sil}}})$ rate, where $p_{\mathrm{sil}}=\log_2(1+\sqrt2)\approx1.2716$, improving upon the classical $O(n^{-1})$ rate of constant-step GD. Although the optimality of $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ has been well supported by numerical evidence for small $n$, a matching lower bound has remained missing. In this paper, we prove an $\Omega(n^{-p_{\mathrm{sil}}-o(1)})$ lower bound for GD, showing that $p_{\mathrm{sil}}$ is the optimal convergence exponent. Additionally, we prove an anytime lower bound that matches the exponent $2p_{\mathrm{sil}}/(1+p_{\mathrm{sil}})\approx1.1195$ of the known upper bound [Zhang, Lee, Du, and Chen, COLT 2025]. Building on the approaches of [Ma and Chen, 2026; Jung, Cho, and Yun, 2026], we select specific iterations as checkpoints at which the GD trajectory explores a new coordinate, and we couple these coordinates using a chain of local functions. Our main technical contribution is a local hard function that bends the GD trajectory between successive checkpoints, resulting in a sharpened lower bound. For each prescribed stepsize schedule, we maximize this bound over admissible checkpoint sets. A recursive analysis of this maximum then yields a lower bound matching the silver exponent for every such schedule.

authors.name: Yuhan Ye, Kaizhao Liu

papers.title: Direct Topology Tracking in Continuous Implicit Models
papers.summary: We present a framework for tracking topological features directly within continuous implicit models. Such models, including implicit neural representations (INRs) and multivariate functional approximations (MFAs), are increasingly adopted to represent scientific data without the resolution constraints of discrete grids. They offer compact, smooth, and differentiable representations of complex fields, enabling new opportunities for high-performance data storage, reconstruction, and analysis. Given a continuous implicit model, our method tracks the evolution of critical points by querying the model and its derivatives, thereby eliminating the need to resample onto a grid. This approach enables faithful feature tracking while avoiding discretization-induced artifacts such as aliasing. We demonstrate the generality of our framework across a range of implicit representations, including analytic functions, MFAs, and INRs, and show that it produces smooth, coherent critical point trajectories. By enabling feature tracking directly on continuous representations, our method supports a new class of feature-driven visualization workflows centered on implicit models.

authors.name: Guanqun Ma, David Lenz, Kaiyuan Tang, Hanqi Guo, Chaoli Wang, Tom Peterka, Bei Wang

papers.title: Are We Grading Properly? Understanding Failure Modes in Medical Benchmarks
papers.summary: Medical evaluation is shifting from static option-based questioning to realistic clinical scenarios with open-ended output modes. Grading these at scale naively, however, is expensive, and rubric-based evaluation has become the dominant scalable alternative. We ask what happens when the rubrics themselves are not airtight, and whether such flaws can be detected and corrected. We apply RIFT, a global rubric failure taxonomy, to three clinical benchmarks (HealthBench Professional, LiveMedBench, and MentalHealthBench), and find failure modes are meaningful: on HealthBench Professional an LLM judge flags 29.6% of criteria as non-atomic and 65.4% as misaligned/rigid, although these rates vary severalfold across five detection judges. Then, we show that these flaws are meaningful and not simply cosmetic. As an example, rewriting bundled criteria of the form "at least one of / all of the following" as equally weighted children and regrading identical responses shifts scores by up to 15.9 percentage points on affected conversations, with disjunctive bundles inflating scores and conjunctive bundles deflating them. Across six answering models and two common graders, these shifts leave the model ranking unchanged, and their net direction depends on how many bundled criteria are penalties. We also find that RIFT can under-detect bundling on clinical rubrics, by an amount that depends on the detection judge: on the same LiveMedBench criteria, judges flag 3.8-15.9% as non-atomic against an estimated 7-19% that are genuinely bundled.

authors.name: Prithvi Dixit, Pedram Hosseini

papers.title: Stop Removing Stopwords: How an Inherited Preprocessing Default Distorts Legal Text-as-Data
papers.summary: Empirical legal scholarship increasingly treats judicial text as data, and much of it still runs on sparse, interpretable pipelines -- TF-IDF features and linear classifiers -- because the textual feature is often the object of study rather than a means to prediction. Yet these pipelines inherit preprocessing defaults from mid-century information retrieval that were never validated against classification accuracy. The most entrenched of these is stopword removal. This study introduces an exhaustive single word ablation that measures the effect of a preprocessing step directly against the downstream objective, and applies it to stopword removal as the hardest case to dislodge. Matching Supreme Court Database labels to Caselaw Access Project opinion texts, the study examines two binary tasks that bracket F1 headroom, ideological direction (no-removal baseline F1 ~0.68) and constitutional versus non-constitutional law type (~0.92), across 7,668 and 7,001 opinions. For each task, the ablation removes each of about 18,500 candidate words in turn, and a task-specific stoplist is built from the measurements. Common generic stoplists fall below the no-removal baseline in all twelve held-out tests. The task-specific stoplists move held-out F1 by +0.0023 (95% CI [-0.0124, +0.0170]) on ideology and by +0.0001 ([-0.0082, +0.0085]) on law type. Neither task shows a detectable benefit from removal, and supplemental analysis finds that word-level statistics predict removal effects poorly, because true removal effects differ by less than the measurement can register, leaving little to predict. The method generalizes to any inherited preprocessing default; the result is a caution specific to interpretable legal text-as-data, where a step that reshapes which features a model sees can distort the doctrinal and ideological signal the research is meant to recover. The burden of proof sits with removal.

authors.name: Gregory M. Dickinson

papers.title: Mammography Foundation Models for Opportunistic Prediction of Major Adverse Cardiovascular Events
papers.summary: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of death among women, yet cardiovascular risk assessment often relies on clinical variables that may be missing, outdated, or unavailable in routine care. Screening mammography offers an opportunity for opportunistic cardiovascular risk stratification because it is routinely acquired and contains vascular features, including breast arterial calcifications (BAC), that are associated with cardiovascular risk and events. We evaluate whether mammography specific foundation models, originally pretrained for breast cancer related tasks, can transfer to cardiovascular risk prediction without cardiovascular specific supervision or explicit BAC annotation. We constructed a 5-year major adverse cardiovascular event (MACE) cohort of 22,497 women linked to electronic health record outcomes, including 500 events (2.22% prevalence).Using only the screening mammogram, the foundation models achieved AUROCs of 0.823 and 0.822, recovering most of the gain of a clinical risk factor model (AUROC 0.859) over an age-only model (0.765), without requiring any clinical variables. Both foundation models evaluated assigned substantially higher predicted risk to patients with radiologist documented BAC, despite BAC never being used as a training label, and showed activation patterns consistent with vascular findings. Together, these findings suggest that mammography foundation models can recover clinically relevant cardiovascular risk information directly from mammographic pixels and suggest that screening mammography may provide an opportunistic source of cardiovascular risk information to complement conventional clinical assessment without additional imaging.

authors.name: Paula Feldman, Nusrat Binta Nizam, Sunwoo Kwak, Batuhan Karaman, Katerina Dodelzon, Mert Sabuncu

papers.title: Swiss-Knife: A Framework for Reconfigurable Externalised Multi-Objective Alignment at Decode Time
papers.summary: Decode-time alignment methods steer a frozen language model by scoring candidate continuations with an external reward and selecting the maximiser. We argue that this shared design is a single degenerate point in a much larger space. We introduce Swiss-Knife, a framework for externalised multi-objective alignment in which the alignment specification is a first-class runtime object: hot-swappable scoring blades, a batch normaliser, a pairwise aggregation operator, and a selection rule. Six axioms characterise the admissible aggregation operators, and we prove a representation theorem: every operator satisfying them has the form $R_i = \sum_{j \neq i} g((\mu_i - \mu_j)/s(\sigma_i,\sigma_j))$, a two-parameter family containing probit and logistic comparison rules and pointwise argmax as named coordinates. Within it, pairwise aggregation is Lipschitz-stable under adversarial reward contamination while argmax is not, and Candidate-Batch Normalization (CBN) makes the weight simplex invariant to the rescalings under which reward models are only ever identified. Our reference instantiation pairs DPO-LoRA blades with an uncertainty-aware pairwise tournament. Sweeping the helpfulness/honesty/harmlessness simplex, it attains the best balanced frontier of six decode-time methods (harmonic $F_1$ 0.797 vs. 0.750 for the strongest baseline, $p < 10^{-14}$) with the lowest refusal rate and highest helpfulness of any arm, and reconfigures its objectives in 0.05 ms with no gradient computation.

authors.name: Agnibh Karmakar, Mayur Parvatikar, Shreyash Dhoot, Amit Dhanda, Aman Chadha, Kapil Wanaskar, Vinija Jain, Amitava Das

papers.title: Visual Jev: Accurate and Efficient Decisions from Shared Visual Context
papers.summary: Applications increasingly ask multiple closed-choice questions about the same image, requiring accurate probabilities and efficient inference. We present Visual Jev, a visual decision model combining LM-head candidate readout, answer-supervised post-training, and independent question branches over a shared visual prefix. On held-out test images from four benchmarks, task SFT raises the 4B model's macro accuracy from 83.4% to 88.5% and error-discrimination AUROC from 0.834 to 0.890. Its macro accuracy exceeds the hosted Jev and OpenAI Decisions APIs by 2.77 and 5.06 percentage points, respectively, with the lowest NLL. We further show that better accuracy and calibration do not ensure reliable decisions. Fixed confidence thresholds exceed target error rates, and simply reordering options changes 17% of the model's accept-or-review decisions on SNLI-VE. At 32 questions per image, shared-prefix inference reduces amortized time per question from 20.5 to 5.6 ms, a 3.7x speedup over batched full sequences on one RTX 5090. Engine-level prefix caching reduces KV memory to 24.3% of that used by our custom shared-prefix path.

authors.name: Guanxu Yu, Yuhang Yao

papers.title: Gradients for Interventions and Activation Values for Detection: Targeted Feature Learning in Language Models
papers.summary: Model-internal features can be studied through both their ability to identify a specified concept and their causal effect when manipulated, e.g., through steering or weight editing. A prominent approach to feature learning is Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), which learn broad feature dictionaries whose relation to particular concepts is typically identified post hoc. However, many interpretability questions are instead hypothesis-driven and concern a concept specified in advance. We study this setting as targeted feature learning, where a single feature is constructed for such a predefined concept. We present a controlled comparison across three model signals (activation values, activation gradients, and parameter gradients) and two estimators (contrastive mean and a learned one-dimensional encoder-decoder), yielding six targeted methods, with CAA and GRADIEND as existing instances and four new methods covering the remaining combinations. We compare these methods against pretrained SAEs across 15 tasks and ten language models, evaluating both detection and causal intervention. Across models, the strongest detection performance is achieved by contrastive activation value methods, whereas the strongest intervention performance is achieved by gradient signals, most strongly with a contrastive mean. Notably, within the contrastive mean family, activation gradients substantially improve intervention over activation values without requiring parameter space interventions. Overall, our results show that targeted feature quality depends jointly on the model signal and estimator, with detection and intervention capturing complementary properties.

authors.name: Jonathan Drechsel, Steffen Herbold

papers.title: Agnostic Smoothed Online Regression with Adversarial Responses
papers.summary:
We study smoothed online prediction with bounded adversarial responses. This widely studied framework bridges i.i.d. sampling and adversarial covariate selection through a smoothness parameter $	extsf{C}_{	extsf{cov}}$, which bounds conditional covariate densities relative to a fixed, unknown base measure. We propose Hedge-Cover, an information-theoretic algorithm that achieves sublinear regret $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{	ext{Pdim}(\mathcal{F}) 	extsf{C}_{	extsf{cov}} T})$ for function classes with bounded pseudo-dimension. The algorithm aggregates a carefully constructed family of experts using Hedge, with a prior that links regret to the number of disagreements between a consistent selector and a target function. We bound this number by exploiting covariate smoothness. This answers an open problem posed in \cite{blanchard2025agnostic} on the minimax optimal adaptive regret of the smoothed online regression problem. We establish a matching lower bound for the class of linear predictors. The main intricacy of the lower bound lies in explicitly constructing a challenging sequential covariate distribution supported on mutually orthogonal hyperplanes. This construction may be of independent technical interest. Finally, we revisit the well-specified setting and quantify the effect of response noise. For conditionally $
u^2$-subGaussian responses, we extend the existing lower bound under realizable responses by showing that the minimax expected regret is $\Omega((1\vee 
u)\sqrt{(	extsf{C}_{	extsf{cov}}-1)dT})$ for a function class of VC dimension $d$. A corresponding upper bound for ERM matches this dependence on $
u$.

authors.name: Xuanyu Chen, Yue Yu

papers.title: The Double-Edged Sword of Information: Revealed versus Hidden Lotteries in School Choice
papers.summary: In school choice, a lottery number is often used by the matching mechanism to break ties when more students prefer the same school than the number of seats available. In practice, in recent years, the NYC Public Schools started revealing the lottery number to students. Theoretical findings from prior literature suggest that revealing the lottery number strictly improves the number of matches under the deferred acceptance algorithm. However, these theoretical results are based on the over-simplifying assumption that all students share the same preference ranking for schools. In this work, we relax this assumption and allow students to have heterogeneous preference rankings. Under a game-theoretic model where student strategies form a Bayesian Nash equilibrium, we characterize scenarios where revealing the lottery number can either improve or worsen the matching outcome, measured by two metrics of the match rate and social welfare, when students submit preference lists of length one. We further consider revealing partial information about the lottery, and demonstrate non-monotonic effects in the amount of information available to students. From these theoretical results, we identify a mechanism through which lottery revealing deteriorates the overall matching quality: Under the revealed lottery, students with weak preferences but high priorities slightly improve their matching outcome at the cost of increasing congestion and substantially worsening the outcome of students with strong preferences. Using a mean-field approximation, we show via simulations that this mechanism continues to operate when the length of preference lists is greater than one. These theoretical and simulation results together illustrate complex tradeoffs induced by the lottery revealing policy, and we identify students' preference heterogeneity and preference intensity as two key factors in shaping these tradeoffs.

authors.name: Parinaz Naghizadeh, Jingyan Wang

papers.title: FlowMap-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Few-Step Flow-Map Generators
papers.summary: Few-step flow-map generators, such as MeanFlow and consistency models, sample in a few long-range jumps. On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on states drawn from its own sampler, but existing methods compare teacher and student through the local stochastic transitions of a multi-step sampler, which a flow-map student never deploys. We present FlowMap-OPD, the first systematic study of OPD for flow-map students. It separates state collection from supervision: the student collects states with its native few-step sampler, while the teacher supervises the flow map, velocities induced from it, or the instantaneous velocity linked to the map by a separately weighted consistency penalty. We find that instantaneous-velocity supervision with a small consistency weight, our chosen form, transfers the teacher's gains best, whereas supervising the deployed map, although the natural choice, transfers them worst when teacher and student start from different pretrained models. This gives a counter-intuitive rule: \emph{sample with the flow map, learn the velocity}. As a further benefit, this form applies to any teacher that defines a velocity, including multi-step ones, and to students initialized from multi-step models. On FLUX and SD3.5, a single few-step student consolidates three specialist teachers within 300 updates, matches or exceeds each on its own benchmark (e.g., OCR 0.883 versus 0.850 on FLUX), and outperforms both multi-reward reinforcement learning and LoRA merging.

authors.name: Zhiqi Li, Cheng Wan, Bo Zhu

papers.title: The sublevel Flood bifiltration: towards scalable 2-parameter persistent homology
papers.summary: Multiparameter persistent homology is a rapidly developing branch of topological data analysis that improves the robustness of single-parameter persistent homology to outliers, while still capturing the metric characteristics of the data. However, a notable limitation is its lack of scalability. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for efficiently computing 2-parameter persistent homology on large point sets. Our work extends the Flood filtration, originally developed for single-parameter persistence. Our construction, called the sublevel Flood bifiltration, offers a scalable approximation of the sublevel offset bifiltration. We show that it benefits from theoretical stability properties and describe how to compute it efficiently. We demonstrate the performance of our approach in classification tasks on low-dimensional synthetic datasets, where density awareness is critical, as well as on real-world time series datasets.

authors.name: Matt\'eo Cl\'emot, Julie Digne, Julien Tierny

papers.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
papers.summary: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.01 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.

authors.name: Chao-Yeh Chen, Tiffany Chen, Lin Duan, Tianyi Hu, Yu-Hsiang Huang, Umar Iqbal, Jiefeng Li, Edy Lim, Yanchen Liu, Yihan Pang, Hang Qiu, Jun Saito, Shao Su, Qingsi Wang, Xiufeng Xie

papers.title: Probing the limits of materials design via a comprehensive crystal database of 14.6 million structures with 140 properties
papers.summary: Forward screening and inverse design drive materials discovery, yet their limits remain unquantified because records of known crystal structures and properties are fragmented across databases. Consequently, forward screening leaves known crystals underexplored for new functions, whereas generative and autonomous discovery has repeatedly reported known phases or close variants as new materials. Here we match structures across 55 databases to assemble MateriaViva, a unified database of 14.6 million distinct crystals and over one billion property values. To provide the missing properties of every structure, a task we term property completion, we develop an equivariant Crystal Graph Transformer Network with state-of-the-art accuracy on nine benchmark tasks and apply 140 property-prediction models across the database. These predictions reveal the underestimated potential of forward screening, identifying tens of thousands of high-performance candidates among previously synthesized or computationally studied materials that lack recorded target-property values. Conversely, comparison with MateriaViva shows that the novelty of inverse design has been overestimated, as 55-100% of inverse-designed structures are not new. Under equal density functional theory verification budgets for bulk-modulus design, inverse design yields a higher fraction of qualifying candidates, whereas forward screening reaches the higher bulk modulus. MateriaViva thus provides a comprehensive reference for probing the limits of both paradigms, revealing unrecognized performance in known crystals and directing inverse design beyond reported structures.

authors.name: Zhilong Song, Zijun Pang, Lixue Cheng

papers.title: How many sorted projections determine any n points in k dimensions?
papers.summary: Let $d_1,\dots,d_m$ be directions in $\mathbb{R}^k$, where $k\ge 2$. A multiset $X$ of $n$ points of $\mathbb{R}^k$ projects to the $m$ multisets of numbers $\{\{x\cdot d_j : x\in X\}\}$, or equivalently to the $m$ sorted lists of these numbers. How many directions are needed for these projections to determine every multiset of $n$ points? Two simple bounds are known in every dimension: more than $(k-1)\log_2 n$ directions are always needed, and $(k-1)n+1$ directions in general position always suffice. In the plane much more is known: Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron showed that almost every choice of $O(\log n \log\log n)$ directions suffices. Whether anything similar holds in higher dimensions was left open by Dym, Wellershoff, Tsoukanis, Levy and Balan. We observe that two lemmas of Hair and Sahai, proved for list recovery of random linear codes, answer that question, and by tightening their argument we show that in every dimension almost every choice of $(4k-2)\ln(2n)\ln(k\log_2 2n)+k+1$ directions suffices. For $k\le 10$ this beats the linear bound once $n$ is larger than about 100: for example, 144 directions suffice for multisets of 1000 points in the plane, and an exact computation lowers this to 133. Letting some of the random blocks in their argument fail removes a factor $\log k$: almost every choice of $O(k\log n\log\log n)$ directions suffices, uniformly in $k$ and $n$. We also show that $2k-1$ directions never determine three points, so that the logarithmic lower bound is not tight; that every $m$ directions in the plane fail on some pair of multisets of size $O(1.65^m)$, improving the bound $O(1.80^m)$ of Matousek, Privetivy and Skovron; and that for each $k$, $m$ and $n$, either almost every choice of $m$ directions works or almost none does.

authors.name: Christopher Gorham Lester, Raymond Hau S{\o}rensen

papers.title: ConDR: Conservative Reachability through Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Subsolutions
papers.summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) Reachability identifies the unsafe states of a dynamical system from which it can be forced into failure under worst-case disturbance. However, classical grid-based solvers scale exponentially with state dimension. DeepReach improves scalability by replacing the grid with a neural value function trained on the HJ-Isaacs (HJI) variational inequality (VI), but penalizes both sides of the residual equally. This allows the learned value to lie above the true one and unsafe states to be misclassified as safe. We propose Conservative DeepReach (ConDR) which aims to learn a subsolution of the HJI VI such that the learned unsafe set contains the true one. ConDR enforces the obstacle branch and terminal condition by construction, pushes the HJI residual to a safety margin $\epsilon$ below zero with a one-sided loss, and prevents the degenerate solution of classifying everything as unsafe. We prove that the exact solution of the margin-shifted VI that ConDR trains toward is a subsolution of the original VI so its unsafe set contains the true one and its value lies within $\epsilon\tau$ of the true value function. We compare against DeepReach and MADR in the established systems of Air3D, Air6D, a 9D multi-vehicle system, and a 13D quadrotor. ConDR reports the lowest rate of unsafe state misclassified and the lowest closed-loop collision rates with at most a small increase in intervention. On Air3D and Air6D, ConDR tolerates model mismatch that scales with $\epsilon$. At matched false-negative rates, ConDR's unsafe sets are smaller than the baselines showing the safety is not obtained by trivial over-approximation.

authors.name: Kendra Givens, Taylor T. Johnson, Bryan C. Ward, Thomas Beckers

papers.title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
papers.summary: Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

authors.name: Zhaohui Xu, Xiaofei Xu, Doudou Zhou

papers.title: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
papers.summary: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. However, blind to the Table of Contents (ToC) as a macro-structure, existing bottom-up paradigms rely on localized visual cues, inducing heuristic fragility in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth; meanwhile, direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding, triggering hallucinations in long contexts. To address this, we introduce TETHER, a training-free framework that elevates the ToC from discarded noise to a vital structural prior, enabling robust adaptation across design-driven long documents. TETHER operates via a two-stage neuro-symbolic mechanism: first, it constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) empowered by spatio-semantic constraints; second, it employs an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to this skeleton, effectively resolving boundary ambiguities. Evaluated across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER delivers highly precise, state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs. Moreover, stress tests highlight TETHER's resilience to sparse omissions and textual noise, demonstrating that its precise semantic alignment is fundamentally anchored in topological and depth fidelity. Crucially, ablations confirm the framework's architectural irreducibility, while achieving 90% token reduction and drastic speedups over end-to-end baselines, establishing a compelling equilibrium between structural precision and deployment scalability.

authors.name: Yu Zou, Yan Chen, Jialei Zeng, Xiaorui Zhou, Aixi Zhong, Qi Zhou, Haoran You, Ke Jiang, Changyu Hu

papers.title: Quantifying Cultural-Psychological Constructs in Four Centuries of Ottoman Court Registers
papers.summary: Populations vary along cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor. But how can these dimensions be studied in historical societies for which conventional psychological data are unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational text-analytic framework for quantifying psychological constructs in 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513-1911 CE. We develop sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language and extend a theory-driven, text-analytic pipeline to capture cultural variation along the dimensions of individualism, collectivism, and honor in this historical corpus. We evaluate our models through multiple methods: document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and validation against expert annotations. Our adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) achieved a Recall@1 of .843 on the test set for document retrieval, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 for semantic textual similarity (meaning the best answer usually appeared as a top result), and classified questionnaire items with 89.58\% accuracy. Document-level performance varied across constructs and methods. Qualitative analysis further showed that high scores reflected historically specific legal and institutional patterns. We publicly release the models, construct representations, scoring pipeline, as well as an interactive web interface to support transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analyses of Ottoman Turkish court records spanning approximately four centuries. These computational tools enable the study of psychological variation across centuries of cultural and institutional change in a diverse empire.

authors.name: Sila Mutaf, Enes Y{\i}landilo\u{g}lu, Mohammad Atari

papers.title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
papers.summary: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

authors.name: Jingyi Sun

papers.title: ChronoDossier: Long-Form Personas as Temporal Memory Representations
papers.summary: Long-horizon agents rely on stored records to recover a person's state as facts change. Reliable answers depend on how facts are recorded, retrieved, and presented to the reader. We treat a long-form persona dossier as a memory representation of a known latent state, an invariant identity plus a timeline of facts, routines, and decision rules tied to life phases. We present ChronoDossier, a benchmark of 311 synthetic dossiers of 1k-10k words written by seven generators from dated timelines. Intrinsic metrics evaluate the records against their intended states; extrinsic metrics test recovery by five readers on a seeded 32-persona GPT-5.1 panel balanced across lengths (520 rated turns per condition). The linked states, records, evidence packets, and answers support tests of construction and evidence delivery. In a contextual-stress control, tag-scoped writer inputs remove detected out-of-scope anchor copying. Frozen questions authored on staged dossiers transfer less reliably to one-pass dossiers of the same states. In matched evidence controls, whole sections repair 29 of 32 GPT-5.1 and 25 of 30 Sonnet 4.6 failures labeled as packaging, compared with 2 of 8 and 1 of 8 answer-formation failures. Attribution uses separate key-based and key-free support measures, with model disagreements retained. Length remains confounded with persona and question composition; the observed between-bucket widening depends on excerpt construction. The benchmark supports offline evaluation against known facts. Memory acquisition from interaction and validation against real users remain outside its scope.

authors.name: Noah Sturgill, Jinho D. Choi

papers.title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
papers.summary: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.

authors.name: Payman Behnam, Elaheh Sobhani, Saad Amin, Yahya Hassan, Daniyal Khan, Biswadeep Chakraborty, Tanish Patwa, Souvik Kundu, Alexey Tumanov

papers.title: PAIR-MED: Policy-reward Alternation for Iterative Refinement in Multilingual Medical Reasoning
papers.summary: Large language models demonstrate strong medical question-answering capabilities, yet reasoning performance remains uneven across languages. Process reward models (PRMs) provide step-level feedback for improving reasoning, but a fixed PRM may become increasingly misaligned with the trajectory distribution of an evolving policy during reinforcement learning, thereby reducing the reliability of its supervision. We propose a policy--reward alternating training framework that jointly adapts a medical PRM and optimizes a multilingual reasoning policy. Following supervised initialization, the current policy generates multilingual trajectories to update the PRM, which then provides process-level rewards for the next policy update. Medical step supervision maintains the PRM's medical foundation, while process, outcome, and language-related rewards guide policy learning. We develop multilingual medical PRMs (PAIR-PRM) and reasoning models (PAIR-MED) at 8B and 9B scales across 12 languages. On the medical subsets of Global-MMLU and MMLU-ProX, our models improve average accuracy by 3.01--7.47% over their corresponding Qwen backbones. On CUREMED-BENCH, PAIR-MED-9B improves the joint language consistency and logical accuracy metric by 12.88% and 7.45% over baselines for in-domain and out-of-domain languages. Further analyses examine PRM adaptation, multilingual reasoning quality, and the contributions of individual training components.

authors.name: Fan Gao, Xiaohang Xu, Lang Huang, Nan Lu, Irene Li

papers.title: PILAPS: A Bilingual Benchmark for Evaluating Pragmatic Inference across Phenomena and Settings
papers.summary: Recent work reports strong pragmatic performance by large language models (LLMs) in English, yet whether this performance generalises across languages and evaluation settings remains unclear. This question is increasingly important as LLMs are deployed across languages, cultures, and conversational contexts. In this paper, we first introduce PILAPS, a bilingual English/Mandarin Chinese benchmark covering eight pragmatic phenomena across purpose-written and dialogue-derived items, with both culturally adapted and independently sourced data. We then evaluate eight LLMs from four families across a range of model sizes and prompting strategies. Our results reveal substantial variation across models and pragmatic phenomena: open-source models continue to struggle particularly with humour, while cross-linguistic performance varies with model origin. Our error analysis shows that, compared with human participants, models are more prone to literal interpretations in conversational contexts. Theory-of-Mind prompting lowers the literal share of errors, whereas Chain-of-Thought prompting slightly raises it. Together, these findings demonstrate that strong pragmatic performance in one evaluation setting does not necessarily generalise across languages or conversational contexts.

authors.name: Jiani Cao, Anna Korhonen, Chen Cecilia Liu

papers.title: DRVEXO-4B-Unified: Design and Evaluation of a Modular Speech-Vision System
papers.summary: We present DRVEXO-4B-Unified, a modular multimodal assistant built around a 4B language backbone. A self-contained checkpoint combines text, image, and speech inputs with reference-conditioned speech output and structured interaction. A temporal residual connector adapts acoustic sequences to the language interface; explicit text boundaries support incremental speech synthesis; and three task-conditioned scoring heads rank supplied action candidates alongside generative tool calls. These interfaces connect conversation to application-defined choices while leaving action authorization to the application. The system obtains 74.22% on all 900 MMMU validation questions, exceeding the published validation scores of Gemma 3 4B IT and InternVL3.5-4B without test-time scaling. Strict prompt-level IFEval accuracy is 82.26% and MATH-500 accuracy is 89.40%, above the original Qwen3-4B non-thinking report's 81.2% and 84.8%, respectively. On NVIDIA GB10, the model achieves a speech-synthesis first-chunk latency of 390 ms. For concurrent text generation, a growth-aware admission policy completes a 128-answer batch at 594.41 output tokens/s, including filling and draining, without preemptions. We plan to release the model weights and accompanying code under Apache License 2.0, retaining applicable third-party terms.

authors.name: Zeyuan Li

papers.title: Rubric Semantics or Numerical Priors? Auditing Scale-Direction Bias in LLM Judges
papers.summary: Recent benchmark evaluations increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as automatic judges. This paradigm assumes LLMs evaluate based on the rubric's semantic meaning rather than its numeric scale. We question this assumption by introducing semantic faithfulness: the principle that semantically equivalent rubrics must yield consistent scores. To quantify this, we propose a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without altering evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we introduce floor normalization to calibrate reversal disagreement against intrinsic model variability, enabling fair cross-model comparisons. Experiments across five meta-evaluation benchmarks with seven diverse LLM judges spanning open-weight and proprietary models reveal widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, showing that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirectional anchor averaging reduces dependence on any single anchor direction without compromising alignment with human judgments. Our findings emphasize that trustworthy LLM judges must reliably follow rubric semantics, not just correlate with human ratings.

authors.name: Chanwoo Kim, Doyun Kim, Minsoo Song, Sihyeon Lee, Chanjun Park

papers.title: TRAC: Efficient Diffusion Language Models for Machine Translation via Length-Aware Decoding
papers.summary: Machine translation with large language models requires both high translation quality and low generation latency. Accelerating translation while preserving quality is therefore essential for practical deployment. Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) can generate tokens at arbitrary target positions through iterative denoising, offering a new paradigm for parallel translation beyond sequential autoregressive decoding. However, existing methods still incur redundant computation: fixed target generation lengths waste computation on unused positions, while confidence-only commitment delays medium-confidence tokens whose predictions have largely stabilized. To address these issues, we propose TRAC, a training-free adaptive decoding method for diffusion machine translation. TRAC adapts the target generation length using source length and translation direction, with a conservative fallback to the maximum length for empty or unusually short outputs. It preserves high-confidence commitment while identifying temporally stable medium-confidence tokens for early commitment using cross-step top-1 persistence and approximate Jensen-Shannon divergence over Top-$K$ distributions. On bidirectional Chinese-English translation across FLORES-200, WMT23, and NTREX-128, TRAC reduces model forward calls by 24.9% to 36.8% and achieves sentence-level generation speedups of 1.91 to 2.19 times over Fast-dLLM, with only a 0.02-point decrease in macro-average COMET. These results demonstrate that adaptive generation lengths and stability-aware token commitment improve the efficiency of diffusion machine translation.

authors.name: Tianyuan Li, Xihan Yang, Chenglong Wang, Yuzhang Wu, Jingbo Zhu, Tong Xiao

papers.title: ColorRef: Calibrating Verbal Feedback for Color Revision
papers.summary: People rarely specify an exact color when asking someone to revise a design: they might say \textit{a little darker} or \textit{more blue} after seeing a proposal. A language-model assistant must then infer not only which way to change the color, but how far. We study this distinction with \textsc{ColorRef}, a color reference game in which a model guesses a color from a description and a teacher, knowing a recorded target hidden from the guesser, supplies verbal corrections. On 1{,}000 crowd-sourced description--target pairs, three rounds of deterministic oracle feedback reduce mean target distance from 42.33 to 22.15 $\Delta E_{76}$. However, those corrections provide additional information, and improvement alone does not establish well-calibrated feedback following. A controlled Qwen3-14B diagnostic reveals a more specific failure: following a requested direction and ordering graded phrases do not guarantee a suitable step size; strong modifiers can induce excessive changes. We therefore measure each receiver's typical response to \textit{a little}, \textit{somewhat}, and \textit{much} on separate colors and select wording matched to its observed steps. On 128 held-out starting colors, calibration reduces one-step mean error from 12.36 to 6.86 for Qwen3-14B and from 11.06 to 5.89 for Gemma 4 12B against a fixed graded-wording rule. The benefit is concentrated on large corrections, with many unchanged cases and no consistent increase in threshold success. Our findings show that following the direction of feedback is not the same as making an appropriately sized revision.

authors.name: Pablo Loyola, Andres Hoyos-Idrobo, Edison Marrese-Taylor, Colin Rowat, Alfredo Solano

papers.title: FoodReact-AR: Learning Audience Reactions that Zero-Shot LLMs Miss in Arabic Food-Insecurity Discourse
papers.summary: Facebook reactions record how an audience received a post, a signal absent from the post's text. We treat the six differentiated reactions on 74,241 Arabic food-insecurity posts from public Facebook pages (2020-2024) as compositions, apply a centered log-ratio transformation, and cluster them into four audience profiles: Solidarity (Love-dominant), Dismissal (Haha-dominant), Grief (Sad-dominant), and a flat Ambivalent profile. Dismissal peaks in 2022 (22.3%), the year of the wheat price shock, and grief in 2024 (14.0%), during the Gaza food emergency; a page-clustered GEE confirms both shifts (odds ratios 2.18 and 1.34), and they survive minimum-reaction filtering, alternative zero replacements and clustering methods, and bootstrap resampling. We then test whether the profiles can be predicted without reactions. A zero-shot Arabic LLM recovers Grief for 83.8% of posts but Dismissal for only 3.4%, and in a matched ablation, it shows the reaction percentages do not help. A simple classifier trained on the reaction-derived labels and tested on unseen pages recovers dismissal for 60.0% (macro-F1 0.56 against 0.43), mainly from mentions of officials and institutions. Derisive audience responses are thus learnable from text, yet a zero-shot LLM misses them. We release the corpus, LLM, and human annotation layers, and an evaluation protocol as FoodReact-AR.
