We construct explicit circuits to perform a logical measurement using the quilt construction, which also require no physical qubits beyond the ancillas already in place to perform idle syndrome extraction on the codeblocks in question. We give a detailed structural analysis of the construction, which is based on a subsystem code, and provide several sets of sufficient conditions under which the relevant code-capacity distance is preserved. We give two variants of the protocol. The first, where the gauge generators of the subsystem code are measured directly, is provably not fault tolerant in the large-distance limit but admits a particularly practical circuit implementation in which the physical qubit degree increases by at most two. The second has more favourable asymptotic properties, although we do not prove its fault tolerance in the general case. We then perform an extensive empirical analysis of the technique, in particular of the first variant, as applied to bivariate bicycle and surface codes, finding code-capacity-distance preserving quilts for measuring 25,000 randomly selected logical operators. We optimise to find sparse and decongested detector bases for each and, for a randomly selected subset, find circuits that we estimate to be distance preserving. Finally, we perform decoding experiments on a subset of these circuits and find that their logical error probability is comparable to that of idle memory for operations involving the 144-qubit bivariate bicycle code and distance-12 rotated surface code at physical error rates between $1.5\times 10^{-3}$ and $3\times 10^{-3}$.

authors.name: Stasiu Wolanski

papers.title: Quantifying the irrealism required by quantum random access codes
papers.summary: How far must decoding observables be from having elements of reality to achieve a given quantum advantage in a communication task? We answer this question for quantum random access codes. Here, an observable has an element of reality when its unrevealed measurement leaves the preparation undisturbed; its irrealism is the relative entropy to the closest such preparation. Because it comprises local coherence and the correlations destroyed by the unrevealed measurement, irrealism applies to prepare-and-measure (PM) and entanglement-assisted (EA) codes alike. For PM codes decoded in mutually unbiased bases, we obtain the irrealism frontier, the least total irrealism compatible with each success probability, exactly in every dimension; an excess-irrealism identity shows that Gibbs states of the decoding operator attain it uniquely. For PM codes minimized also over the decoders, the required irrealism vanishes up to the classical value and is positive beyond it; for qubits, mutually unbiased decoders are not the cheapest below a success probability of 0.833. For EA codes with a qubit receiver, trusted decoders, and parity-dependent sender settings, the frontier exceeds the PM one by the realism-based nonlocality of the contexts used by an optimal code, and with rank-one projective sender measurements a success probability above 0.815 certifies a minimum realism-based nonlocality of the shared state.

authors.name: Pedro R. Dieguez

papers.title: Entanglement, records, and quantum recovery in qubit chains
papers.summary: We investigate entanglement, readable records and quantum recovery using an exactly solvable chain of sequentially interacting qubits. For weak interactions, entanglement reaches a later environment site before that site carries an equally strong local record. The leading local record is encoded in an off-diagonal element of the reduced density matrix and can be detected by a Pauli measurement, while a population measurement gives a higher-order signal. We further characterize the accessibility of the relative phase through joint transverse correlations and derive the optimal fidelity for recovering an unknown quantum state from the system and an accessible environment fragment. We show that interactions acting only within the environment can redistribute readable records and change the region required for quantum recovery without affecting the reduced state of the system.

authors.name: Sugumi Kanno, Jiro Soda

papers.title: Effect of coupling asymmetry on the spontaneous decay and entanglement of two atoms in a common cavity
papers.summary: We investigate the dynamics and the spontaneous decay of two identical two-level atoms into the vacuum in a cavity at low temperature. We analytically derive the survival probability and the amplitudes of the state of the system by calculating the exact self-energy when the atoms are both initially excited. It is found that moderate asymmetry enhances the decay of the survival probability and increases the entanglement production in either lossless and lossy cavities.

authors.name: Yamen Hamdouni

papers.title: Efficient Classical Algorithms for Ground Energy Estimation of Fermions with Conjugate-Pair Orbital Interactions
papers.summary: Estimating the ground energy of interacting fermions is central to quantum many-body physics, and recent quantum algorithms provide polynomial-time guarantees for some structured families. Classical approaches commonly rely on quantum Monte Carlo, where the sign problem is a major obstacle. However, even when a nonnegative expansion without sign problem is available, rigorous guarantees for rapid mixing are still far from well understood. In this paper, we give an efficient classical randomized algorithm for approximating the ground energy of fermionic Hamiltonians with conjugate hopping matrices and conjugate-paired orbital interactions, which includes the attractive Hubbard models. This guarantee not only holds without a physical spectral gap or a weak-coupling assumption, but also covers interactions beyond onsite density attractions. Technically, we first reduce ground-energy estimation to partition-function estimation and then use a discretization with controlled energy error to obtain a nonnegative weighted sum of squared determinant moduli and then apply the Chen--Liu log-concave counting theorem. In addition, we obtain a sharper arithmetic bound by controlling how many independent sampling runs and matrix updates are needed, and using sparse matrices to reduce the cost of each update.

authors.name: Ziyi Yang, Yexin Zhang, Yuexin Su, Xinzhao Wang, Xiaoyang Wang, Tongyang Li

papers.title: Non-Binary Detector Error Models
papers.summary: A key challenge in fault-tolerant quantum error correction (QEC) is that the syndrome extraction circuits are themselves faulty. Such circuit-level noise is commonly described by a detector error model (DEM). In Stim and in almost all related works, DEMs are binary: every non-binary circuit error (e.g., CNOT gate), is decomposed into independent binary error mechanisms. In this work, we introduce non-binary DEMs, in which each fault location of the syndrome extraction circuit is modeled by one random variable over its original alphabet, e.g., the 16 two-qubit Pauli errors after a CNOT gate. We also propose a split-merge-regroup transformation that builds a compact non-binary DEM from any Clifford circuit by merging the error components that flip the same detectors and observables. Non-binary DEMs represent any Pauli channel exactly, whereas binary DEMs are exact only for channels that factorize into independent binary parts. When the channels factorize, we prove that binary and non-binary DEMs are equivalent under degenerate quantum maximum-a-posteriori (MAP) decoding, but not under quantum MAP decoding. Although the variables are non-binary, belief propagation (BP) still exchanges a single scalar message per edge. Our numerical results with surface, color and bivariate bicycle codes show that non-binary DEMs have two main advantages. First, their Tanner graphs have four to five times fewer edges, which is advantageous for hardware implementations. Second, their performance under BP, with and without OSD post-processing, is better than that of their binary counterparts, and BP with OSD runs up to $9.4\times$ faster in a CPU.

authors.name: Stefano Tinelli, Francisco L\'azaro, Francisco Garc\'ia Herrero

papers.title: Tunable Ground-State Entanglement in Fully Connected Quantum Systems: From Logarithmic to Volume-Law Scaling
papers.summary: Entanglement scaling is a central probe of the complexity of quantum many-body ground states, yet once geometric locality is absent, it can depend sensitively on the structure and normalization of interactions. For fully connected Hamiltonians with the natural Kac normalization, nondegenerate gapped ground states are known to obey a logarithmic entanglement bound. Here we ask how the ground-state entanglement changes when this interaction normalization is continuously relaxed away from the Kac scale. We answer this question by constructing an explicit all-to-all bipartite Hamiltonian of $n$ qubits with Fourier pairing amplitudes and pairwise interaction strength proportional to $n^{-\kappa}$. For sufficiently small fixed coupling, we prove that every pure ground state has entanglement entropy $\Theta(n^{2-2\kappa} \log n)$ for $1/2<\kappa\leq1$ and $\Theta(n)$ at $\kappa=1/2$. We further show that the ground state is unique and separated from the rest of the spectrum by a system-size-independent gap for $3/4 \leq \kappa \leq 1$, while weak-coupling analysis and numerical calculations suggest that the gap remains open also for $1/2 \leq \kappa < 3/4$. Thus, varying only the interaction normalization yields a controlled hierarchy from logarithmic scaling at the natural Kac normalization $\kappa=1$ to increasingly strong subextensive entanglement and ultimately to a volume law, showing that even an arbitrarily weak relaxation of this normalization precludes a universal logarithmic entanglement bound.

authors.name: Donghoon Kim, Tomotaka Kuwahara

papers.title: When lies look like noise: certifying untrusted entanglement swapping
papers.summary: Entanglement swapping lets quantum repeaters distribute entanglement over long distances, a prerequisite for the quantum internet. We study its security in a noisy network whose intermediate nodes perform the quantum operations faithfully but may misreport the classical outcome that end users rely on. We show that the ideal functionality of entanglement swapping cannot be realised, because it gives the adversary no influence over the delivered state, whereas a node that relabels its report does have such influence. Including honest noise in the ideal setting does not help unless it also concedes a bounded fraction of misreported pairs. We therefore propose a cut-and-choose protocol that tests a random subset of pairs to certify the rest. Since no test can distinguish a misreport from readout noise, the protocol certifies the error above a pre-agreed minimum noise level, which is the misreport rate under our threat model. This yields a quality-of-service guarantee, in which a failure witnesses that the node did not deliver as agreed. Unlike verification schemes that consume the state they certify, the untested pairs remain available for use, with a finite-size guarantee. Certifying a 1% misreport rate on 10^6 pairs costs 10^4 to 1.7x10^5 test pairs, for minimum noise levels ranging from 0 to 5%. The main cost is memory, since 1% requires holding 10^5 to 10^6 pairs at once, far beyond the capacity of today's quantum memories. Verifying and releasing in blocks ties the memory to the block size at the cost of a weaker rate: a (10^4)-qubit memory certifies 14% on 4.7x10^5 delivered pairs.

authors.name: Maria Gragera Garces, Chris Heunen, Mahesh K. Marina

papers.title: Optimal Error corrected Hamiltonian estimation with nuisance parameters
papers.summary: Realistic quantum sensing is often affected by both noise and unknown nuisance parameters. Under Markovian dynamics, existing error correction approaches have often sought to suppress nuisance responses alongside environmental noise. Here we show that this local suppression of nuisance parameters is unnecessary and can be overly restrictive: nuisance parameters and Markovian noise impose fundamentally different constraints and require distinct treatments. We establish a general framework for quantum sensing with parameters encoded in a general time dependent Hamiltonian, in the presence of both nuisance parameters and Markovian noise. We derive a necessary and sufficient condition for Heisenberg scaling, determine the exact optimal precision, and construct protocols that attain it. Our results show that to achieve Heisenberg scaling Markovian noise must be suppressed locally by quantum error correction, whereas nuisance parameters need not, and in general should not, be eliminated locally. Instead, optimally designed coherent control can separate their accumulated effects from the target signal over the full sensing evolution. Consequently, Heisenberg scaling can remain attainable even when the target signal is instantaneously aligned with nuisance parameter directions, in sharp contrast to alignment with Markovian noise. This distinction substantially enlarges the regime in which Heisenberg scaling is attainable and provides a general principle for designing robust quantum sensors.

authors.name: Zhiyao Hu, Haidong Yuan, Liang Jiang, Zain H. Saleem

papers.title: When the Noise Gets Noisy: Quantum Error Correction with Disordered Noise and Misinformed Decoding
papers.summary: Experimental demonstrations of quantum error correction often exhibit noise that varies across space and time, and attempting to characterize this disorder has been shown to substantially improve decoding performance. However, theoretical studies of quantum error correction typically assume fixed, perfectly known, homogeneous noise. Here we model decoding with incomplete or inaccurate knowledge of disordered noise channels by treating physical error rates as random variables. We show that the decoding performance is set by a small number of information-theoretic functionals of the noise distribution: the entropy determines the threshold while Bhattacharyya coefficients bound the deep sub-threshold decay rate of logical failures. Furthermore, our results give a quantitative measure of the benefits of characterizing this noise. We numerically investigate both maximum-likelihood and minimum-weight-error decoding of surface codes, showing good agreement with theory across the code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise settings, including with noise distributions seen in open-access superconducting devices. When it comes to error correction in realistic settings, reporting the average entropy and Bhattacharyya coefficient of noise distributions could therefore be more informative than the mean or median error rates of a device's components.

authors.name: Cory T. Aitchison, Lucas H. English, Benjamin B\'eri, Dominic J. Williamson, Campbell K. McLauchlan

papers.title: Hamiltonian Stabilization of the Two-Photon Dicke Model
papers.summary: Collective two-photon light--matter interactions enable pair amplification but can destroy spectral confinement, preventing a stable thermodynamic bright phase. We show that a positive Kac-scaled number-Kerr interaction renders the two-photon Dicke Hamiltonian of \(N\) emitters lower-bounded at all couplings while preserving its generalized \(\mathbb Z_4\) symmetry. We determine the exact zero-temperature thermodynamic energy density with \(O(N^{-1})\) finite-size control and obtain the global phase diagram. A bright minimum is born at a saddle-node and exchanges global stability with the normal minimum at coexistence, producing a discontinuous photon-density jump. Symmetry-resolved exact diagonalization through \(N=128\) supports the predicted density jump and an exponentially closing same-sector normal--bright tunneling gap. Spectral collapse thus becomes the singular zero-Kerr point of a first-order phase diagram, identifying a Hamiltonian route to stabilizing pair amplification.

authors.name: Pradip Laha, Kingshuk Adhikary, Subhashish Banerjee, Peter van Loock

papers.title: On the design of sequential quantum repeaters with error detection
papers.summary: Long-distance, trust-free quantum communications rely on the development of scalable quantum repeater schemes. Sequential entanglement generation with error detection is a promising approach that combines manageable implementation requirements with a hop-by-hop architecture compatible with existing classical infrastructure. In this paper, we investigate key design choices for such schemes over a repeater chain using quantum key distribution as a benchmark. We find that simple quantum error-detecting codes, such as repetition codes or quantum parity codes, perform well under near-term hardware assumptions and outperform strategies without any encoding. In particular, we show that two-qubit repetition codes may well be all that we need to implement in many practical scenarios. We also examine different architectures for the generation of initial entanglement and assess their merits. Additionally, we show that moderate improvements in some hardware components can partially mitigate the slow technological progress of others.

authors.name: Javier Rey-Dom\'inguez, Koji Azuma, Mohsen Razavi

papers.title: Authenticating quantum key distribution through random position checks
papers.summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) requires some form of authentication in order for the parties to be sure they are not unknowingly generating a key with an adversary pretending to be one of the honest parties. In this work, we propose a protocol in which the position of one of the parties is used as the authentication credential for key distribution. Our protocol essentially consists of a BB84 QKD protocol with quantum position verification (QPV) rounds randomly interleaved in. The approach is efficient compared with previous approaches, which required running an entire QPV protocol for every bit requiring authentication. We undertake an initial security analysis of the protocol for a restricted set of attacks.

authors.name: Florian J. Curchod, Erik Woodhead, Cameron Foreman, Marcel Mordarski, Harry Buhrman

papers.title: Classical Oracle Separation of QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy and Quantum Cryptography Even When P = QCMA
papers.summary: Remark: This work is in submission at STOC'27 and thus the full manuscript has been publicly posted on the conference website since November 3rd, 2026. Inspired by the Codeword-Hash Structure problem recently introduced by Cakan (arXiV, 2026) to separate $\mathsf{QMA}$ from $\mathsf{QCIP}$, we introduce a new problem called Codeword-Hash pairs in Noise ($\mathsf{CHN}$) and prove that, in the query complexity model, it is in $\mathsf{QMA}$ but hard for the $\mathsf{QCMA}$ hierarchy $\mathsf{QCMAH} = \bigcup_{d\geq1}\mathsf{QCMA}^{\mathsf{QCMA}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{QCMA}}}}$, the classical-witness quantum-verifier analogue of $\mathsf{PH}=\bigcup_{d\ge1}\mathsf{NP}^{\mathsf{NP}^{\cdots^{\mathsf{NP}}}}$. Using this problem, we show that there exists a classical oracle ${O}$ such that $\mathsf{P}^{{O}}=\mathsf{BQP}^{{O}}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{{O}} =\mathsf{QCMAH}^{{O}} \subset \mathsf{QMA}^{{O}} \text{ but } \mathsf{QMA}^{{O}}\not\subseteq\mathsf{QCMAH}^{{O}},$ thus showing that quantum state or quantum proof advantage could exist even if classical computers can efficiently solve any problem that can be quantumly verified with a classical proof. Further, using our problem, we show that various quantum cryptographic primitives can exist even when $\mathsf{P} = \mathsf{QCMA}$ and thus neither quantum-computable one-way functions nor (verifiable) quantum computational advantage exist. In particular, relative to a classical oracle ${O}$ with $\mathsf{P}^{{O}}=\mathsf{BQP}^{{O}}=\mathsf{QCMA}^{{O}}=\mathsf{QCMAH}^{{O}}$, there exist pseudorandom states with classical keys and public-key encryption with copy-protected quantum decryption keys and classical public keys and ciphertexts, among other primitives, answering an open question of Kretschmer, Qian, and Tal (STOC 2025).

authors.name: Alper Cakan

papers.title: Classically Trained Quantum Generative Models with Shared Training and Fine Tuning for Quantum Matter
papers.summary: Ground-state measurement statistics characterize quantum matter. Selected correlations can guide the classical training of a quantum sampler even when sampling the full distribution is difficult. We ask whether training across related ground-state distributions helps the sampler reproduce their correlations more accurately. We train a hypernetwork to map Hamiltonian parameters to circuit angles, sharing information across the phase diagram before local fine-tuning with additional reference data for quantum deployment. For classical training, we derive an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator of Fourier coefficients for circuits built from general Pauli rotations, with a cost that depends on the circuit generators. We also introduce a CDF-KL loss for comparing selected marginals. We study the Haldane Hamiltonian and transverse-field Ising model, using an automated search to select reference calculations near phase transitions. On the twelve-site chain, the adaptively pretrained hypernetwork matches the independent fits' final mean total variation distance in fewer local updates and continues to a lower error. On a 1,024-site chain and a 4 by 256 lattice, the fine-tuned circuits have lower squared maximum mean discrepancy from the reference distributions than the independent circuits at the evaluated point in each geometry. These results motivate shared training for preparing quantum samplers across a phase diagram and local fine-tuning.

authors.name: Mario Herrero-Gonzalez, Elham Kashefi, Mina Doosti

papers.title: End-to-End Quantum Algorithm for Differential Equations: Application to Simulating a Biomolecular System
papers.summary: Quantum algorithms for differential equations have the potential for substantial algorithmic speedups over classical methods. However, they rely on certain assumptions and abstract oracle specifications that leave their practical feasibility and computational advantages for realistic applications unclear. Here we formalize the concept of an end-to-end quantum algorithm for differential equations as one that accepts classical inputs and returns classical outputs, and provide implementations for algorithmic primitives in constructing such algorithms. We present a tailored end-to-end quantum algorithm for the linearized Poisson-Boltzmann (LPB) equation, a partial differential equation (PDE) with variable coefficients widely used in simulating a biomolecular system. We explicitly implement all aspects of the algorithm, from preparing an initial state to generating a quantum solution and estimating properties of the system. In particular, we develop a new discrete representation for variable-coefficient PDEs on a grid that enables efficient implementation of the operator oracle, and build on a recent technique based on optimal wavelet preconditioning to generate a quantum solution with a cost independent of the condition number of the discretized operator. We show the algorithm can be implemented by quantum circuits of size polylogarithmic in both the number of grid points $N_g$ and the inverse of the desired accuracy $\varepsilon$, with an overall gate cost polylogarithmic in $N_g$ and quasilinear in $1/\varepsilon$. We also show the classical preprocessing to construct the circuits has polylogarithmic cost in $N_g$ and $1/\varepsilon$. Our work provides a concrete end-to-end quantum algorithm for a PDE of practical value, demonstrates an exponential improvement in scaling with $N_g$ over classical methods, and provides a foundation for assessing its potential quantum advantage in practice.

authors.name: Mohsen Bagherimehrab, Daniyaal Farooqi, Gavin K. Brennen, Barry C. Sanders, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik

papers.title: Fast, in-place, and ancilla-free quantum algorithms for integer multiplication and inversion
papers.summary: Arithmetic operations are a fundamental building block in the design of quantum algorithms, with their implementation cost expected to have a significant impact on the viability of a wide variety of quantum applications. In this work, we present novel algorithms for a number of in-place quantum arithmetic operations that are highly efficient in terms of their space and gate count overheads compared to the current state-of-the-art. We show that in-place modular multiplication of integers, modulo a power of two, can be performed with either a classical or quantum odd multiplier using $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $\epsilon >0$. We then show that standard in-place integer multiplication can be performed with a non-zero classical or quantum multiplier using $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ gates for any $\epsilon>0$, with no ancilla qubits required for the classical multiplier and a logarithmic number of ancilla qubits for the quantum. Using our quantum modular multiplication algorithm, we also show that in-place modular inversion, modulo a power of two, can be performed using $O(n^{1+\epsilon})$ gates and no ancilla qubits, for any $\epsilon>0$. To our knowledge, these are the first quantum algorithms achieving both subquadratic gate counts and sublinear ancilla counts for each of the considered in-place operations. All but one of these fast operations are optimal in terms of memory, only requiring enough space to store the output of the operation, which overwrites the input directly. We present our multiplication algorithms as consequences of a single unified theorem, which may find further application within quantum arithmetic.

authors.name: David Halpenny, Adithya Sireesh, Petros Wallden

papers.title: Query-Optimal Quantum Minimum Finding from Numerical Estimators
papers.summary: We propose a quantum minimum-finding algorithm for objectives accessed via numerical estimators that avoids the logarithmic query overhead of amplifying the confidence of estimates before the search. A coherent estimator that is $\varepsilon$-accurate with probability at least $2/3$ on each of $N$ labels suffices to find a $2\varepsilon$-optimal label using $O(\sqrt N)$ base-estimator queries at constant confidence. The query bound and the additive-error constant are separately worst-case optimal. More generally, suppose a preparation assigns probability mass at least a known $p$ to objective values at most $a$. Without knowing $a$ or the prepared distribution, our algorithm returns a candidate and an estimate $v$ such that, jointly with constant probability, $v$ is $\varepsilon$-accurate for the candidate and $v\le a+\varepsilon$. The algorithm uses $O(p^{-1/2})$ queries to each of the preparation and estimator oracles in the worst case, and the selected candidate can be retained as a quantum state. For preparation width $s_P$ and estimator workspace width $w$, it requires $O(s_P+w+\log\log(4/p))$ qubits, independently of the requested confidence. Applications give worst-case optimal $\Theta(\sqrt N/\eta)$ queries for selecting an $\eta$-optimal bounded expectation, and guided ground-energy estimation using $O(\omega^{-1})$ preparations and $O((\omega\eta)^{-1})$ elementary controlled-evolution queries at constant confidence, where $\omega$ is a lower bound on the guiding state's ground-space amplitude overlap.

authors.name: Egil Bae

papers.title: High-temperature Gibbs states are uniformly Markovian and trivial
papers.summary: We prove that, above a constant temperature threshold, Gibbs states of local noncommuting qudit Hamiltonians exhibit exponential decay of mutual information and conditional mutual information (CMI). Specifically, we prove exponential decay of the CMI for arbitrary spatial tripartitions $A \sqcup B \sqcup C$ which need not comprise the entire system, thereby establishing a \textit{uniform Markov property} for high-temperature Gibbs states. A central obstruction to proving such bounds is that conventional cluster expansions for the logarithm of reduced Gibbs states can fail to converge due to noncommutativity. Our main insight is to construct a classical representation of the Gibbs state using an overcomplete basis. Although such representations generally involve negative quasiprobability weights, we show that a decomposition based on projective 2-designs admits a convergent cluster expansion with strictly positive weights at sufficiently high temperatures, allowing us to circumvent the obstruction. The separability of high-temperature Gibbs states is a natural byproduct of this decomposition. Finally, in the context of mixed-state phases of matter, our results imply that high-temperature Gibbs states belong to the same mixed-state phase as the maximally mixed state.

authors.name: Andrew D. Kim, Tai Hsuan Yang, Jong Yeon Lee

papers.title: Quantum many-body scars and zero modes in the spin-1 Kitaev chain
papers.summary: We study the spin-1 Kitaev chain and, by analyzing its Hilbert-space connectivity in the Cartesian basis, show that it hosts an exponentially large number of exact zero-energy modes protected by chiral symmetry. For even-length periodic chains, their count is lower-bounded by the Jacobsthal number $(2^{L+1}+1)/3$, where $L$ is the chain length. We then construct an exponentially large number ($2^{L/2}$) of zero modes with an analytic expression that have a maximally mixed density matrix for a contiguous bipartition using the operator-state mapping. We further identify an embedded tight-binding structure governing defect dynamics that supports PXP-like quantum many-body scars (QMBS) in multiple sectors previously not reported. The associated forward-scattering approximation (FSA) Hamiltonian takes a universal form across the scarred sectors studied. A simple physical picture of defects propagating between walls provides an intuitive description of these dynamics and a structural guide to identifying sectors with fidelity revivals, while its limitations point to additional scarring mechanisms.

authors.name: Ayush Sharma, Jay Pandey

papers.title: Compiling Constraints into Neuromorphic Ising Machines
papers.summary: Most practical combinatorial optimization problems involve constraints, and an Ising machine that flips one spin at a time can respect them only through energy penalties that raise barriers between feasible solutions. Here we show that a higher-order neuromorphic Ising machine can enforce constraints through programmable transitions rather than penalties. In an autoencoder-like architecture, each inner-layer neuron represents a move, a family of multi-spin transitions that maps every feasible state to another feasible state, receives the energy change of its move through connections that outer-layer neurons multiplicatively switch on or off, and updates the state through the same connections. A compiler turns constraints into this wiring with a number of auxiliary clauses that grows only polynomially for parity, cardinality, one-hot, partition and permutation constraints. Restricting the search to feasible states reduces constraint handling to move design, and we show that the fastest-annealing moves are not those that mix fastest but those that lower the deepest energy barriers, and that moves chosen from the objective lower them further than random ones. On third-order graph matching, the machine needs orders of magnitude fewer iterations than penalty-based neuromorphic machines. Configured as a sampler on a field-programmable gate array, it decodes the surface code with maximum-likelihood accuracy up to code distance 15 within 52 $\mu$s per shot and, under noisy syndrome measurements, decodes in real time for millisecond measurement rounds up to distance 9 with fewer logical errors than belief-propagation decoders.

authors.name: Faiek Ahsan, Shantanu Chakrabartty

papers.title: Momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo for twisted bilayer graphene: Interaction effects in the presence of remote bands
papers.summary: Twisted bilayer graphene hosts strong correlation effects within topological flat bands separated from remote dispersive bands. This separation motivates projection onto the central bands, which greatly reduces the computational complexity of many-body calculations, including momentum-space quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations. However, the interaction-induced Mott gap obtained in the projected model can be comparable to the noninteracting flat--remote band separation, raising the question of whether the projection remains valid. Here, we extend momentum-space QMC to explicitly include remote BM bands within a broad energy window at charge neutrality. We find that the projected description remains reliable over a broad parameter regime, up to $u_0/u_1\lesssim0.9$: the projected and remote-band calculations yield similar low-energy electron and trion spectra, and the Kramers intervalley-coherent ground state remains stable. In particular, the Dirac trion remains robust in the finite-temperature normal state when remote bands are included. Near the band-touching limit $u_0=u_1$, remote-band electrons acquire substantial low-energy spectral weight, accompanied by suppression of the trion weight and loss of the Kramers intervalley-coherent state. Our findings establish the broad validity of flat-band projection while reconciling the projected and THF viewpoints by identifying the near-band-touching regime in which explicit remote-band degrees of freedom become essential.

authors.name: Shibo Shan, Cheng Huang, Zi Yang Meng

papers.title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Transition
papers.summary: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.

authors.name: Xin Jin, Maximillian Liao, Handong Chen, Yi Nancy Li, Junyu Liu

papers.title: Precise experimental investigation of the reflection properties caused by s-polarized evanescent waves and the Casimir puzzle
papers.summary: We report a high-precision experiment on measuring the low-frequency magnetic field reflected from a metallic plate. This experiment is designed to give insight into why theoretical predictions of the fundamental Lifshitz theory using the standard response function to the electromagnetic waves are in contradiction with the data of numerous precision measurements of the Casimir force (the Casimir puzzle). To attain these ends, we measured the magnitude and phase of the lateral component of the magnetic field produced by an oscillating magnetic dipole and reflected from a metallic plate. These quantities are completely determined by the evanescent waves with the transverse electric (s) polarization. The obtained measurement data are compared with theoretical predictions using the standard Drude response function of the metal to the low-frequency electromagnetic waves. It is shown that there are both quantitative and qualitative disagreements with these predictions, so that in the region of low-frequency s-polarized evanescent waves the Drude response function is excluded by the data. Keeping in mind that just the s-polarized evanescent waves are responsible for the Casimir puzzle, our results highlight the causes for its emergence. It is emphasized that, in addition to the Casimir effect, searching for the adequate nonlocal response functions of metals to the evanescent waves is of utmost significance for many areas of physics as near-field optical microscopy, nanophotonics, surface plasmon polaritons, radiative heat transfer, and others.

authors.name: M. Dhital, G. L. Klimchitskaya, V. M. Mostepanenko, U. Mohideen

papers.title: Genuinely Out-of-Equilibrium Bose-Einstein Condensation
papers.summary: Bose-Einstein (BE) condensation typically occurs in the ground state. Prominent exceptions include excitons, whose ground state is the vacuum; consequently, they undergo BE condensation only in out-of-equilibrium regimes to counteract rapid decay. Here, we develop a driven-dissipative framework to address this challenge, demonstrating that BE condensates emerge under sufficiently strong excitation in one and two dimensions. In three dimensions, by incorporating effective loss rates and a specified injection energy, we find a percent-level condensate fraction, consistent in order of magnitude with the exciton experiment of Morita et al. (Nat. Commun. 13, 5388 (2022)).

authors.name: Tatsuhiko N. Ikeda, Masahito Ueda

papers.title: Imaginary-Time Density Correlations Encode Quantum Entropy and Free Energy
papers.summary: In the classical limit, maximum-entropy inference yields an estimate of the excess entropy from the static structure factor through a single momentum sum. Quantum mechanically this estimate fails, because interactions also change the kinetic energy, while delocalization and exchange add information that equal-time correlations do not contain. We show that imaginary-time density correlations contain this information, and that with them the classical relation carries over to quantum systems. Such correlations are available from path-integral simulations and X-ray Thomson scattering. Relative-entropy inference over imaginary-time paths, with an ideal Bose or Fermi gas as reference, gives closed forms for the excess entropy and free energies, within the same Gaussian approximation as the classical relation. They recover the classical result and estimate entropy that the classical relation misses. We test them on weakly interacting bosons, interacting fermions on a ring, and the warm dense electron gas. The closed forms need only imaginary-time density correlations and their ideal-gas reference at a single state point, without using the interaction potential. Our approach can extend other classical entropy estimators to quantum systems.

authors.name: Sagi Meir

papers.title: Scalable Simulation of Strongly Correlated Fermions with Neural Gaussian Tensor Networks
papers.summary: Accurate simulations of strongly correlated electrons remain a central challenge in computational physics. We introduce neural-network Gaussian projected entangled-pair states (NN-GPEPS), which exploit the locally-entangled subspace of Gaussian states to give an architecture more compatible with modern neural networks and an exact contraction cost of $O(N^{3/2})$ on two-dimensional lattices. For the Hubbard model at $U/t=8$ and $1/8$ hole doping, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies in large lattices of up to 1024 sites. These results demonstrate an accurate approach to strongly correlated fermions by connecting neural networks with Gaussian tensor networks.

authors.name: Runze Chi, Ao Chen, Garnet Kin-Lic Chan

papers.title: Quadratic Models for Engineered Control of Open Quantum Systems
papers.summary: We introduce a framework to model the evolution of a class of open quantum systems whose environments periodically undergo an instantaneous non-unitary evolution stage. For the special case of quadratic models, we show how this approach can generalise the formalism of repeated interactions to allow for the preservation of system-environment correlations. Furthermore, its continuous zero-period limit provides a natural description of the evolution of small systems coupled to large environments in negligibly perturbed steady states. We explore the advantages and limitations of this approach in illustrative applications to thermalisation in a simple hopping ring and to the problem of initialising a qubit chain via environmental engineering.

authors.name: J. P. P. Vieira, A. Lazarides, T. Ala-Nissila

papers.title: Symmetries, correlation functions, and entanglement of general quantum Motzkin spin-chains
papers.summary: Motzkin spin-chains, which include `colorless' (integer spin $s=1$) and `colorful' ($s \geq 2$) variants, are one-dimensional (1D) local integer spin models notable for their lack of a conformal field theory (CFT) description of their low-energy physics, despite being gapless. The colorful variants are particularly unusual, as they exhibit power-law violation of the area-law of entanglement entropy (as $\sqrt{n}$ in system size $n$), rather than a logarithmic violation as seen in a CFT. In this work, we analytically discover several unique properties of these models, potentially suggesting a new universality class for their low-energy physics. We identify a complex structure of symmetries and unexpected scaling behavior in spin-spin correlations, which deviate from known 1D universality classes. Specifically, the $s=1$ chain exhibits $U(1)$ spontaneous symmetry breaking and ferromagnetic order. Meanwhile, the $s \geq 2$ chains do not appear to spontaneously break any symmetries, but display quasi-long-range algebraic order with power-law decaying correlations, inconsistent with standard Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) critical exponents. We also derive asymptotic scaling expressions, with explicit additive constants, for entanglement measures in both colorless and colorful chains, generalizing previous results of Movassagh [J. Math Phys. (2017)], while providing benchmarks for potential quantum simulation experiments. The $\sqrt{n}$ entanglement scaling implies that any matrix-product-state description of these ground states requires bond dimension $e^{\Omega(\sqrt{n})}$; this superpolynomial cost of the standard 1D tensor-network toolkit, along with the analytical tractability of their ground state properties, positions Motzkin spin chains as intriguing testbeds for quantum simulation of many-body physics.

authors.name: Varun Menon, Andi Gu, Ramis Movassagh

papers.title: Kerr-Induced Impairments in Quantum-Classical Fiber Coexistence: A Quantum-Stochastic Analysis
papers.summary: Quantum and classical optical signals sharing a fiber can interact through Kerr cross-phase modulation without interchannel photon transfer, potentially degrading phase- and mode-sensitive quantum communication even when direct spectral leakage is negligible. We develop a two-channel quantum-stochastic propagation framework based on the positive-P representation for a weak coherent pulse train co-propagating with a strong, quadrature-amplitude-modulated classical signal. Both fields are treated quantum mechanically, incorporating self- and cross-phase modulation, chromatic dispersion, group-velocity mismatch, attenuation, and Kerr-induced quantum diffusion. We characterize the classical-channel influence using three complementary observables: the frequency-resolved quadrature-fluctuation spectrum, complex temporal-mode overlap, and adjacent-pulse interference visibility. Simulations of a 100-km standard-fiber link reveal markedly different responses across these observables. As classical launch power increases, the extremal quadrature-fluctuation spectra remain close to the shot-noise level, whereas the temporal-mode and visibility penalties reach approximately 4.5% and 6.0%, respectively, at 100 mW. Applying a 1% mean-penalty criterion gives launch-power thresholds of approximately 46 mW for temporal-mode overlap and 40 mW for visibility, yielding a joint Kerr-limited threshold near 40 mW for the investigated configuration. These results demonstrate that temporal-mode deformation and reduced pulse-to-pulse coherence can occur while the evaluated quadrature-fluctuation spectra remain near shot noise, establishing a complementary criterion for selecting classical launch power in quantum-classical fiber co-propagation.

authors.name: Sumit Chaudhary, Shahram Dehdashti, Igor Litvin, Janis N\"otzel

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Quantum Error Correction: A Comprehensive Review
papers.summary: Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is the process of detecting and correcting errors in quantum systems, which are prone to decoherence and quantum noise. QEC is crucial for developing stable and highly accurate quantum computing systems, therefore, several research efforts have been made to develop the best QEC strategy. Recently, Google's breakthrough shows great potential to improve the accuracy of the existing error correction methods. This survey provides a comprehensive review of advancements in the use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools to enhance QEC schemes for existing Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum (NISQ) systems. Specifically, we focus on machine learning (ML) strategies and span from unsupervised, supervised, semi-supervised, to reinforcement learning methods. It is clear from the evidence, that these methods have recently shown superior efficiency and accuracy in the QEC pipeline compared to conventional approaches. Our review covers more than 150 relevant studies, offering a comprehensive overview of progress and perspective in this field. We organized the reviewed literature on the basis of the AI strategies employed and improvements in error correction performance. We also discuss challenges ahead such as data sparsity caused by limited quantum error datasets and scalability issues as the number of quantum bits (qubits) in quantum systems kept increasing very fast. We conclude the paper with summary of existing works and future research directions aimed at deeper integration of AI techniques into QEC strategies.

authors.name: Zihao Wang, Hao Tang

papers.title: Atoms, Worldlines, and the Scalar Approximation
papers.summary: The worldline path-integral method, developed thus far for scalar fields, offers promising computational efficiency in general geometries, However, it relies so far on the scalar approximation that decomposes electromagnetic waves into two independent polarizations. In this work, we investigate different theoretical frameworks of fluctuation-induced effects and analyze the limitations of the worldline path-integral method in modeling multiple-atom Casimir-Polder interactions. In particular, we ask the question: how accurate is the scalar approximation? Using the worldline approach, it appears that a simple sum of the contributions from the two polarizations agrees with the exact Casimir-Polder force for two-atom systems. However, it turns out that this agreement is fortuitous. To enable calculations beyond two atoms via worldlines, we develop general N-atom expressions for the Casimir-Polder force within the scalar approximation. For three-body systems, the scalar worldline method fails drastically, predicting significant discrepancies in both magnitude and sign due to strong polarization mixing. Furthermore, we show that the TE/TM decomposition in the worldline method differs from that of the Green-tensor formalism, and we discuss why this is. This study highlights the inadequacy of scalar worldline models that rely on the polarization-decomposition approximation in general geometries.

authors.name: He Zheng, Daniel A. Steck

papers.title: Arbitrary Boundary Conditions and Constraints in Quantum Algorithms for Differential Equations via Penalty Projections
papers.summary: Complicated boundary conditions are essential to accurately describe phenomena arising in nature and engineering. Recently, the investigation of a potential speedup through quantum algorithms in simulating the governing ordinary and partial differential equations of such phenomena has gained increasing attention. We propose an approach to enforce arbitrary boundary conditions and constraints through adding a penalty projection to the governing equations, relying on known quantum differential equation solvers, leading to an overall efficient quantum algorithm for solving differential equations under boundary conditions and constraints. Assuming a fast-forwardable representation of the projection to ensure an efficient interaction picture simulation, the cost to enforce the constraints is at most $O(\log \lambda)$ in the strength of the penalty $\lambda$ in the gate complexity within the scenarios we considered, for precision $\varepsilon$ and a dynamical system generated by $A_0(t)$ of size $n^d \times n^d$ with forcing $b(t)$. E.g., for the heat equation, this leads roughly to a gate complexity overhead of $\widetilde O(d \log n + \log t)$. We show constraint error bounds for the penalty approach,both constraint and solution error, and provide validating numerical experiments, and estimate the circuit complexity using the Linear Combination of Hamiltonian Simulation.

authors.name: Philipp Schleich, Tyler Kharazi, Xiangyu Li, Jin-Peng Liu, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik, Nathan Wiebe

papers.title: Ultracold Mechanical Quantum Sensor for Tests of New Physics
papers.summary: Initialization of mechanical modes in the quantum ground state is crucial for their use in quantum information and quantum sensing protocols. In quantum processors, impurity of the modes' initial state affects the infidelity of subsequent quantum algorithms. In quantum sensors, excitations out of the ground state contribute to the noise of the detector, and their prevalence puts a bound on rare events that deposit energy into the mechanical modes. In this work, we measure the excited-state populations of GHz-frequency modes in a high-overtone bulk acoustic wave resonator (HBAR). We find that the population of the first excited state can be as low as $P_p$=(1.2$\pm$5.5)$\times10^{-5}$, corresponding to an effective temperature of 25.2 mK, which are upper bounds limited by imperfections in the measurement process. These results compare favorably to the lowest populations measured in superconducting circuits. Finally, we use the measured populations to constrain the amplitude of high-frequency gravitational waves, the kinetic mixing strength of ultra-light dark matter, and non-linear modifications of the Schr\"{o}dinger equation describing wavefunction collapse mechanisms. Our work establishes HBARs as a versatile resource for quantum state initialization and studies of fundamental physics.

authors.name: Andraz Omahen, Simon Storz, Marius Bild, Dario Scheiwiller, Matteo Fadel, Yiwen Chu

papers.title: Simulating and Sampling from Quantum Circuits with 2D Tensor Networks
papers.summary: Classical simulations of quantum circuits play a vital role in the development of quantum computers and for taking the temperature of the field. Here, we classically simulate various physically-motivated circuits using 2D tensor network ans\"atze for the many-body wavefunction which match the geometry of the underlying quantum processor. We then employ a generalized version of the boundary Matrix Product State contraction algorithm to controllably generate samples from the resultant tensor network states. Our approach allows us to systematically converge both the quality of the final state and the samples drawn from it to the true distribution defined by the circuit, with GPU hardware providing us with significant speedups over CPU hardware. With these methods, we simulate the largest local unitary Jastrow ansatz circuit taken from recent IBM experiments to numerical precision. We also study a domain-wall quench in a two-dimensional discrete-time Heisenberg model on large heavy-hex and rotated square lattices, which reflect IBM's and Google's latest quantum processors respectively. We observe a rapid buildup of complex loop correlations on the Google Willow geometry which significantly impact the local properties of the system. Meanwhile, we find loop correlations build up extremely slowly on heavy-hex processors and have almost negligible impact on the local properties of the system, even at large circuit depths. Our results underscore the role the geometry of the quantum processor plays in classical simulability.

authors.name: Manuel S. Rudolph, Joseph Tindall

papers.title: A Modular PyTheus Quantum Network Interpreter: Automated Analysis and Visualization of Optimized Quantum Architectures
papers.summary: We present a modular interpreter for PyTheus-optimized quantum networks that automatically analyzes and visualizes complex quantum architectures discovered through automated optimization. The interpreter addresses the critical challenge of understanding machine-designed quantum networks by providing robust algorithms for functional role identification, graph-theoretical analysis, and physically meaningful visualization across the major classes of PyTheus-generated networks. Our interpreter accepts both file-based and in-memory network representations, automatically identifies sources, detectors, beam splitters, and ancillas through priority-based classification, and generates coordinated native graph plots and optical table representations. We demonstrate the interpreter's capabilities through two complementary approaches: (1) analysis of a newly developed five-node quantum key distribution network that reveals distributed source architecture and dual-role node functionality, and (2) comprehensive validation using existing PyTheus examples including W4 state generation, heralded Bell state preparation, and GHZ state networks. The interpreter successfully handles complex connectivity patterns across diverse quantum network architectures within the tested classes, avoids visualization artifacts, and provides validation mechanisms for architectural consistency. Our primary contribution is the development of robust modular interpretation algorithms that can analyze the major classes of PyTheus-generated quantum networks, enabling better understanding of automated quantum architecture design.

authors.name: S. K. Rithvik

papers.title: Projected evolution of quantum gates for circuit simulation with matrix product states
papers.summary: Tensor networks and specifically matrix product states (MPS) enable feasible classical quantum circuit simulation when entanglement remains compressible, but for this, gate updates must balance accuracy, representation size, and runtime. Conventional methods incorporate a complete gate into the MPS before compressing enlarged bonds. Here, we instead use lessons from the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) to analyze the projected action of each gate on the MPS by reducing it to a continuous generator path. We establish the spatial and state-space structure of this projected evolution and show that both the fixed-rank and two-site actions are confined to a contiguous window spanned by the gate while retaining boundary information from the surrounding MPS. Within this window characterization, we delineate when the instantaneous two-site action is exact and when variational directions can block it completely. Using standard nearest-point-projection geometry, we also show that fixed-rank TDVP and the local nearest fixed-rank projection of the exact gate endpoint agree to first order. We implement the gate-window restriction with rank-adaptive two-site TDVP and test both the projected update and a hybrid method that reserves it for long-range gates. Across the circuit benchmarks, these implementations incur runtime overhead and show no consistent accuracy--cost advantage over the tested baseline methods. The resulting framework provides a gate-specific structural analysis and a tested implementation together with explicit limits on its practical performance.

authors.name: Aaron Sander, Maximilian Fr\"ohlich, Mazen Ali, Martin Eigel, Jens Eisert, Michael Hinterm\"uller, Christian B. Mendl, Richard M. Milbradt, Robert Wille

papers.title: Optimal phase change for a generalized Grover's algorithm
papers.summary: We study the generalized Grover's algorithm with an arbitrary amplitude vector to find the optimal phase change for maximizing the gain in probability for the target of each iteration. In the classic setting of Grover's algorithm with a real initial amplitude vector, we find that a phase change of $\pi$ stays optimal until the probability of observing the target is quite close to 1. We provide a formula for identifying this cut-off point based on the size of the data set. When the amplitude is truly complex, we find that the optimal phase change depends non-trivially on the complexity of the amplitude vector. We provide an optimization formula to identify the required optimal phase change.

authors.name: Christopher Cardullo, Min Kang

papers.title: Verifiable Quantum Advantage via Optimized DQI Circuits
papers.summary: Recently, a quantum algorithm called Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) was introduced that achieves an apparent exponential speedup for Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) problem, which has previously been studied in the contexts of cryptography and error correcting codes. However, this left open the question of how many logical gates and logical qubits would be needed to solve a classically intractable instance of OPI. Here, we develop optimized implementations of DQI which greatly reduce its resource requirements. We establish that DQI for OPI is the first known candidate for verifiable quantum advantage with optimal asymptotic speedup: solving instances with classical hardness $O(2^N)$ requires only $\widetilde{O}(N)$ quantum gates, matching the theoretical lower bound. To realize this, we overcome the primary bottleneck of reversible Reed-Solomon decoding by introducing novel quantum circuits for the Extended Euclidean Algorithm (EEA) on degree-$n$ polynomials with $b$-bit coefficients that reduce the leading-order space complexity to $2nb$ qubits. These improvements are broadly applicable, including to Shor's algorithm for the discrete logarithm. We analyze OPI over binary extension fields $\mathrm{GF}(2^b)$, assess hardness against new classical attacks, and identify resilient instances. Our resource estimates show that classically intractable OPI instances (requiring $>10^{23}$ classical trials) can be solved with approximately 5.72 million Toffoli gates per shot and $1885$ logical qubits. This is roughly $100$ times fewer gates than required for factoring RSA-2048 and, remarkably, is also less than the leading interactive protocol for computational proof of quantumness, positioning DQI as a compelling candidate for practical, verifiable quantum advantage.

authors.name: Tanuj Khattar, Noah Shutty, Craig Gidney, Adam Zalcman, Noureldin Yosri, Dmitri Maslov, Ryan Babbush, Stephen P. Jordan

papers.title: Enhancing Kerr-Cat Qubit Coherence with Engineered Dissipation
papers.summary: Quantum computing crucially relies on maintaining quantum coherence for the duration of a calculation. Bosonic quantum error correction protects this coherence by encoding qubits into superpositions of noise-resilient oscillator states. In the case of the Kerr-cat qubit (KCQ), these states derive their stability from being the quasi-degenerate ground states of an engineered Hamiltonian in a driven nonlinear oscillator. KCQs are experimentally compatible with on-chip architectures and high-fidelity operations, making them promising candidates for a scalable bosonic quantum processor. However, their bit-flip time must increase further to fully leverage these advantages. Here, we present direct evidence that the bit-flip time in a KCQ is limited by leakage out of the qubit manifold and experimentally mitigate this process. We coherently control the leakage population and measure it to be > 9%, twelve times higher than in the undriven system. We then cool this population back into the KCQ manifold with engineered single-photon dissipation, identify conditions under which this suppresses bit-flips, and demonstrate increased bit-flip times up to 3.6 milliseconds. By employing both Hamiltonian confinement and engineered dissipation, our experiment realizes dissipative stabilization of a KCQ. Our results elucidate the interplay between these stabilization processes and indicate a path towards fully realizing the potential of these qubits for quantum error correction.

authors.name: Francesco Adinolfi, Daniel Z. Haxell, Alessandro Bruno, Laurent Michaud, Venus Hasanuzzaman Kamrul, Preeti Pandey, Alexander Grimm

papers.title: Many-body $k$-local ground states as probes for unitary quantum metrology
papers.summary: Multipartite quantum states saturating the Heisenberg limit of sensitivity typically require full-body interactions to be prepared. On the other hand, experimentally practical Hamiltonians often involve few-body correlators only. Here, we study the metrological performances under this constraint, using tools derived from the quantum Fisher information. Our work applies to any encoding generator, also including a dependence on the parameter. For moderate system sizes up to hundred spins (even), we find that symmetric ground states of Hamiltonians with significantly few-body interactions exhibit an average quantum Fisher information that agrees with that of Haar-random symmetric states and displays Heisenberg-like scaling sensitivity. We also discuss the interaction requirements to generate metrologically useful Haar-random symmetric eigenstates. Finally, we establish a tradeoff between the Hamiltonian's gap, which quantifies preparation hardness, and the quantum Fisher information of the corresponding ground state.

authors.name: Majid Hassani, Mengyao Hu, Guillem M\"uller-Rigat, Matteo Fadel, Jordi Tura

papers.title: Quantum Anticodes
papers.summary: This work introduces a symplectic framework for quantum error correcting codes in which local structure is analyzed through an anticode perspective. In this setting, a code is treated as a symplectic space, and anticodes arise as maximal symplectic subspaces whose elements vanish on a prescribed set of components, providing a natural quantum analogue of their classical counterparts. This framework encompasses several families of quantum codes, including stabilizer and subsystem codes, provides a natural extension of generalized distances in quantum codes, and yields new invariants that capture local algebraic and combinatorial features. The notion of anticodes also naturally leads to operations such as puncturing and shortening for symplectic codes, which in turn provide algebraic interpretations of key phenomena in quantum error correction, such as the cleaning lemma and complementary recovery. It also yields new descriptions of weight enumerators, including a quantum analogue of Greene's theorem relating weight enumerators to polymatroid invariants.

authors.name: ChunJun Cao, Giuseppe Cotardo, Brad Lackey

papers.title: In-situ benchmarking of fault-tolerant quantum circuits. I. Clifford circuits
papers.summary: Benchmarking physical devices and verifying logical algorithms are important tasks for scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing. Numerous protocols exist for benchmarking devices before running actual algorithms. In this work, we show that both physical and logical errors of fault-tolerant circuits can even be characterized in-situ using syndrome data. To achieve this, we map general fault-tolerant Clifford circuits to subsystem codes using the spacetime code formalism and develop a scheme for estimating Pauli noise in Clifford circuits using syndrome data. We give necessary and sufficient conditions for the learnability of physical and logical noise from given syndrome data, and show that we can accurately predict logical fidelities from the same data. Importantly, our approach requires only a polynomial sample size, even when the logical error rate is exponentially suppressed by the code distance, and thus gives an exponential advantage against methods that use only logical data such as direct fidelity estimation. We demonstrate the practical applicability of our methods in various scenarios using synthetic data as well as the experimental data from a recent demonstration of fault-tolerant circuits by Bluvstein et al. [Nature 626, 7997 (2024)]. Our methods provide an efficient, in-situ way of characterizing a fault-tolerant quantum computer to help gate calibration, improve decoding accuracy, and verify logical circuits.

authors.name: Xiao Xiao, Dominik Hangleiter, Dolev Bluvstein, Mikhail D. Lukin, Michael J. Gullans

papers.title: Fault-tolerant execution of error-corrected quantum algorithms
papers.summary: Scaling up quantum algorithms to tackle high-impact problems in science and industry requires quantum error correction and fault tolerance. While progress has been made in experimentally realizing error-corrected primitives, the end-to-end execution of logical quantum algorithms using only fault-tolerant (FT) components has remained out of reach. We demonstrate the FT and error-corrected execution of two quantum algorithms, the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and the Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd (HHL) algorithm applied to the Poisson equation, on Quantinuum H2 and Helios trapped-ion quantum processors using the $[[7,1,3]]$ Steane code. For QAOA circuits on 5 and 6 logical qubits, we show performance improvements from increasing the number of QAOA layers and the number of $T$ gates used to approximate logical rotations, despite increased physical circuit complexity. We further show that QAOA circuits with up to 8 logical qubits and 9 logical $T$ gates perform similarly to unencoded circuits. For the largest QAOA circuits we run, with 12 logical (97 physical) qubits and 2132 physical two-qubit gates, we still observe better-than-random performance. Finally, we show that adding active QEC cycles and increasing the repeat-until-success limit of state preparation subroutines can improve the performance of a quantum algorithm, thereby demonstrating critical capabilities of scalable FT quantum computation. Our results are enabled by a FT logical $T$ gate implementation with an infidelity of $2.7(4)\times10^{-3}$ and dynamic circuits with measurement-dependent feedback. Our work demonstrates near-break-even performance of complex, error-corrected algorithmic quantum circuits using only FT components.

authors.name: Michael A. Perlin, Zichang He, Anthony Alexiades Armenakas, Pablo Andres-Martinez, Tianyi Hao, Dylan A. Herman, Yuwei Jin, Karl Mayer, Chris N. Self, David Amaro, Ciaran Ryan-Anderson, Ruslan Shaydulin

papers.title: Optimal Continuous- to Discrete-Variable Bipartite Entanglement Conversion
papers.summary: Discrete-variable (DV) entanglement is crucial for numerous quantum applications, yet its deterministic generation in many bosonic systems remains experimentally challenging. In contrast, continuous-variable (CV) entanglement can be produced efficiently. We propose two optimal schemes for converting CV bipartite entanglement into DV entanglement using only local operations and classical communication. The first scheme extracts maximally entangled qubit pairs at the theoretically maximal rate, while the second probabilistically produces a maximally entangled qudit pair with the highest average entanglement. In both schemes, we quantify the optimal performance and identify the measurement operators required for implementation. Notably, using only a sequence of binary measurements, our approach can succeed in a finite number of measurement rounds on average, even though the CV resource is infinite-dimensional. Our schemes improve the feasibility of implementing DV-based quantum technologies on bosonic platforms.

authors.name: Pak-Tik Fong, Ruchir Tullu, Hoi-Kwan Lau

papers.title: p-Adic Dirac Equations and the Jackiw-Rebbi Model
papers.summary: We present a p-adic version of the Jackiw-Rebbi model, in which the real line is replaced by the p-adic numbers and the Dirac Hamiltonian by a non-local operator built from the twisted Vladimirov operator. We show that p-adic quantum mechanics, although non-local, yields a physical picture that agrees with the Archimedean one, realized through mechanisms with no Archimedean counterpart. The agreement is specific: for a constant mass the p-adic model is gapped, with the same gap; it has a chiral symmetry, so its spectrum is symmetric about zero energy; a change of sign of the mass binds states at an interface; and at low energies its spectrum cannot be distinguished from the Archimedean continuous spectrum. The mechanisms are not: the p-adic free Hamiltonian is diagonalized by compactly supported wavelets, so every stationary state is strictly localized; momentum takes values on a geometric ladder of powers of the prime; and a zero-energy interface state exists only for masses commensurate with that ladder. The standard Dirac equation does not admit space-localized solutions because it contradicts Einstein's causality. The model is realizable at every finite resolution, as a continuous-time quantum walk, and the topological protection of the Archimedean zero mode is lost.

authors.name: W. A. Z\'u\~niga-Galindo

papers.title: The Spectrum Lies: Level Repulsion in Open Quantum Systems Lacks Physical Meaning
papers.summary: In Hamiltonian systems, level statistics provide a faithful diagnostic of quantum chaos. By analogy, Lindbladian spectral statistics are widely used for open quantum systems, following the Grobe-Haake-Sommers conjecture that systems with chaotic classical counterparts exhibit level repulsion. Here we identify a fundamental limitation of this analogy. Unlike Hamiltonian spectra, the Lindbladian spectral bulk contributes little to long-time dynamics, which are governed by modes with real parts closest to zero. Bulk modes typically decay on microscopic time scales unless concentrated near the imaginary axis. Consequently, perturbations must influence the dynamics before these modes decay to produce observable effects. Yet level statistics resolve much finer spectral scales, allowing perturbations to alter spectral correlations without appreciably changing evolution. Strong Lindbladian non-normality amplifies this separation, enabling drastic changes in level statistics under dynamically negligible perturbations. We demonstrate examples exhibiting Ginibre level repulsion without signatures of dynamical chaos at any time. Moreover, we construct pairs of Lindbladians whose dynamics become indistinguishable for all observables and times in the thermodynamic limit, despite displaying contrasting spectral statistics, with and without level repulsion. Our results challenge Lindbladian bulk statistics as universal chaos diagnostics, suggesting possible reliability only for approximately normal generators with spectra concentrated near the imaginary axis.

authors.name: Caio B. Naves, Thomas Klein Kvorning, Jonas Larson

papers.title: Explainable quantum regression algorithm with encoded data structure
papers.summary: Hybrid variational quantum algorithms are promising for solving practical problems, such as combinatorial optimization, quantum chemistry simulation, quantum machine learning, and quantum error correction on noisy quantum computers. However, variational quantum algorithms (derived from randomized hardware-efficient ansatz or adaptive ansatz) become a black box, not trustworthy for model interpretation, and not to mention for application deployment in informing critical decisions. In this paper, we construct the first interpretable quantum regression algorithm, in which the quantum state exactly encodes the classical data table and the variational parameters correspond directly to the regression coefficients, which are real numbers by construction, providing a high degree of model interpretability and minimal cost to optimize due to the right expressiveness. We also exploit the encoded data structure to reduce the gate complexity of computing the regression map. To reduce circuit depth in nonlinear regression, our algorithm can be extended by directly constructing nonlinear features via classical preprocessing, such as independent encoded column vectors. By design, the model performance is determined by the cost function measurement results $\mathcal{C}$ synchronous to the mean squared errors (MSE) for the regression models. We derived the read-out errors induced by one-hot encoding and compact encoding; the required physical qubit resources are exponentially compressed for the compact encoding to be favorable for noisy quantum devices. We also derive the cost function dependent sample complexity $ \in \mathcal{O}\left(\sigma^{2}(\mathcal{C}) \ln (1/\alpha)/\epsilon^{2}\right)$ under the error budget $\epsilon$ and confidence tolerance $\alpha$.

authors.name: C. -C. Joseph Wang, F. Perkkola, I. Salmenper\"a, A. Meijer-van de Griend, J. K. Nurminen

papers.title: Systematic frequency-collision analysis of the cross-resonance gate outside the straddling regime
papers.summary: Frequency crowding remains a major obstacle to scaling fixed-frequency transmon processors. Among the widely used all-microwave two-qubit gates, the cross-resonance (CR) gate is particularly sensitive to qubit-frequency spread because the conventional straddling regime condition constrains assignable qubit frequencies tightly and makes the system susceptible to frequency collisions. Here, we present a systematic framework for frequency-collision analysis and frequency-allocation optimization, focusing on the CR gate outside the straddling regime, which we refer to as the far-detuned regime. We numerically characterize frequency collisions among qubits through systematic parameter sweeps and identify collision-free conditions. We then optimize frequency allocation using mixed-integer programming on a unit-cell lattice with periodic boundary conditions. We demonstrate that far-detuned designs significantly reduce collisions compared with designs in the straddling regime. Monte Carlo yield analysis indicates that a 10% collision-free yield for a 1024-qubit square lattice at a 0.1% two-qubit-gate error threshold requires $\sigma_{\mathrm{f}}/2\pi \le 6.86~\mathrm{MHz}$. Our frequency-allocation optimization framework could also be useful for other two-qubit gates based on fixed-frequency qubits.

authors.name: Shinichi Inoue, Shotaro Shirai, Shuhei Tamate, Shu Watanabe, Kohei Matsuura, Rui Li, Yasunobu Nakamura

papers.title: Non-Maximally Entangled States for Quantum Key Distribution in Underwater Channels: BBM92 Protocol via Kraus Operators
papers.summary: Underwater optical channels pose significant challenges to the security and reliability of quantum communication systems due to absorption and scattering. In this paper, we investigate the BBM92 entanglement-based quantum key distribution (EBQKD) protocol under realistic conditions over a non-turbulent underwater channel. Photon pairs are prepared in non-maximally entangled states, and the underwater propagation medium is modeled as a quantum channel composed of a polarization-independent photon-loss channel and a depolarizing channel, described within the Kraus operator formalism. The protocol performance is evaluated in terms of quantum correlations, quantum bit error rate (QBER) and secret key rate (SKR), analyzed as functions of the entanglement degree and channel degradation parameters. We derived analytical expressions for the quantum correlations, the QBER and the SKR over the proposed channel model, and validated them through Monte Carlo simulations. The proposed framework is then applied to various realistic underwater scenarios, considering different water types, namely clear ocean, coastal, and turbid water, as well as varying atmospheric conditions.

authors.name: Nour Rizk, Ang\'elique Dr\'emeau, Arnaud Coatanhay

papers.title: RELIQ: Optimizing Parallel Execution of Commuting Pauli Product Rotations
papers.summary: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation (FTQC) permits parallel execution of mutually commuting Pauli Product Rotations (PPRs), but per-qubit access point/port limits (e.g. two X and two Z edges on the surface code) force commuting groups that exceed the budget to execute sequentially, inflating circuit depth. We show that minimizing this hardware-limited depth is NP-hard and propose two heuristics for reducing it: 1. port-aware list scheduling, which reorders commuting PPRs by placing each PPR in the earliest group that can still accommodate it, and 2. generator restructuring, which rewrites each group as an equivalent generating set with reduced per-qubit port pressure. On QASMBench circuits compiled to PPRs, we combine the two heuristics in RELIQ (Restructure + List schedule Quantum circuits) and observe an average hardware-limited depth reduction of 76.3% and 79.1% for Clifford + T and Clifford + Rz circuits, respectively, over a non-reordering baseline. These gains persist as the per-qubit port budget grows, with RELIQ still reducing the depth by 71.7% and 51.2% at $16$ ports, suggesting these heuristics remain relevant even as hardware exposes more access points.

authors.name: Sayam Sethi, Devika Nambisan, Jonathan Mark Baker

papers.title: Exact Solution for Non-Hermitian Free Fermions: A Case Study of the XY Chain
papers.summary: We study the non-Hermitian XY spin chain with open boundary conditions and complex anisotropy. We express its quasi-energies and mode eigenvectors in a Chebyshev-polynomial representation using the quasi-energy as the spectral variable. For finite even $L$, we prove that every exceptional point is of second order. Each Chebyshev sector can contain at most one double root at fixed coupling, and the two sectors cannot become defective simultaneously. Retaining the boundary residual allows the associated generalized eigenvectors to be obtained by differentiation, giving the Jordan structure and the counting of ordinary and generalized many-body eigenstates. For the explicit $L=4$ case, the energy and eigenvector branches exhibit the characteristic square-root monodromy. The normalized left-right overlap is identified with the phase rigidity, whose vanishing corresponds to a divergent eigenvalue condition number. These results provide an exact treatment of defective eigensystems and their local spectral sensitivity within a quadratic fermionic model.

authors.name: Yuguan Li, D. C. Liu, Murray T. Batchelor

papers.title: Quantification of Entanglement in Three-Qubit Systems
